"![](images/ea/ea36f1ec1ddeb03dd8d133fb8d65b5d50b3fa07ba34495978d87f95742dee042.png)

The diagram above shows the region of integration. It consists of two type I regions, given by

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le x\}\,\cup \,\{(x,y)\,:\,2\le x\le 4,\,0\le y\le 4-x\}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the left boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x),$ is

$$
y=x\,⟹\,x=y
$$

and the right boundary of the region is

$$
y=4-x\,⟹\,x=4-y.
$$

To change the order of integration we write $D$ as a type II region. The type II representation of the region is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,y\le x\le 4-y\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/e8/e82098a4bb63f1d709a06b6a24da078594716d6a3cc0fa2e069af9dcd9154955.png)

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{x}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{2}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{4-x}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{y}^{4-y}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186129189 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-18010b03-c75c-5a16-8ddc-495cf577e016" "question-1781d10d-4447-567d-8dfd-9f16c098a159"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-18010b03-c75c-5a16-8ddc-495cf577e016" :question/id #uuid "18010b03-c75c-5a16-8ddc-495cf577e016" :question/math-academy-id "q-38799" :question/problem "${\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{x}^{1}{x}^{2}{e}^{{y}^{4}}\text{d}y\,\text{d}x=$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/54/54727a51e88b3543726b61606a0f41b9a8cf5ec46ef4c69d7233fd54a4b50242.png)

The diagram above shows the region of integration. This is a type I region, and its type I representation is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,x\le y\le 1\}.
$$

Notice that the left boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x)$ is

$$
x=0,
$$

and the right boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x),$ is

$$
y=x\,⟹\,x=y.
$$

To change the order of integration, we write $D$ as type II region. Its type II representation is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,0\le x\le y\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/95/956aaf81973d9a2b3e56082ecae8e654eee55d6f99c42dd433d126632d7c7262.png)

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{x}^{1}{x}^{2}{e}^{{y}^{4}}\text{d}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{y}{x}^{2}{e}^{{y}^{4}}\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{{y}^{4}}[{\int }_{0}^{y}{x}^{2}\text{d}x]\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{{e}^{{y}^{4}}}{3}[{x}^{3}]_{0}^{y}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{3}\,{e}^{{y}^{4}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{12}{[{e}^{{y}^{4}}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{12}(e-1).\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-7eba9098-a15f-5710-a728-b6dfa4ffcdb7"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id :question/math-academy-id "q-82253" :question/problem "By changing the order of integration in the following double integrals, express the following sum as a single double integral.

$$
{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2{x}^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{4-2x}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x
$$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/83/8359a189981b238d0851324a896ed0a3a9aa0620e8cf4d38228752ff484b4cd0.png)

The diagram above shows the region of integration. It consists of two type I regions, given by

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 2{x}^{2}\}\,\cup \,\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 2(x-2)^{2}\}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the left boundary of the region, written in the form $y=y(x),$ is

$$
y=2{x}^{2}\,⟹\,x=\sqrt{\frac{y}{2}}
$$

and the right boundary of the region is

$$
y=4-2x\,⟹\,x=\frac{4-y}{2}.
$$

To change the order of integration we write $D$ as a type II region. The type II representation of the region is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,\sqrt{\frac{y}{2}}\le x\le \frac{4-y}{2}\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/be/bee5de8ca9011672a159686d1547a909e5288097b15241f5004e5c788459ee70.png)

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2{x}^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2(x-2)^{2}}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{\sqrt{y/2}}^{(4-y)/2}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-7dc9b43e-629a-5bba-b51a-3bf554da7329"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186388293 :question/worked-solution "![](images/34/3426e7bdd134bc9af5a3665f8c9c55a65514afa9dca5be112eabb37479c4c9ec.png)

The diagram above shows the region of integration. It consists of two type II regions, given by

$$
\begin{aligned}D & =\{(x,y)\,:\,1-e\le y\le 0,\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-y)\le x\le 1\}\,\cup \,\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le e-1,\,\operatorname{ln}⁡(y+1)\le x\le 1\}.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the top boundary of the region, written in the form $x=x(y),$ is

$$
x=\operatorname{ln}⁡(y+1)\,⟹\,y={e}^{x}-1,
$$

and the bottom boundary of the region is

$$
x=\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-y)\,⟹\,y=1-{e}^{x}.
$$

To change the order of integration, we write $D$ as a type I region. The type I representation of the region is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,1-{e}^{x}\le y\le {e}^{x}-1\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/7d/7d88d351b481859ec3e77350d3679387836d2e7f67325caca50e2f61cce9dcce.png)

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1-e}^{0}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡(1-y)}^{1}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y+{\int }_{0}^{e-1}{\int }_{\operatorname{ln}⁡(y+1)}^{1}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{1-{e}^{x}}^{{e}^{x}-1}f(x,y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-1781d10d-4447-567d-8dfd-9f16c098a159" :question/id #uuid "1781d10d-4447-567d-8dfd-9f16c098a159" :question/math-academy-id "q-132647" :question/problem "${\int }_{-4}^{-1}{\int }_{1}^{-4/y}\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡x-x+2}}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y=$" :question/worked-solution "![](images/d2/d2ef7f656cf706636c82e1ef41ae338a596fff5142962a74875f762301937932.png)

The diagram above shows the region of integration. It is a type II region, and its type II representation is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,-4\le y\le -1,\,1\le x\le -\frac{4}{y}\}.
$$

Notice that the top boundary of the region, written in the form $x=x(y),$ is

$$
y=-1,
$$

and the bottom boundary of the region is

$$
x=-\frac{4}{y}\,⟹\,y=-\frac{4}{x},
$$

To change the order of integration, we write $D$ as a type I region. The type I representation of the region is

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le x\le 4,\,-\frac{4}{x}\le y\le -1\},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](images/33/3338ee0f8bdc6f18bb5a56b12a36d31d79c87db6c39686adc7ae7c00efb9d526.png)

Therefore, swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-4}^{-1}{\int }_{1}^{-4/y}\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡x-x+2}}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{-4/x}^{-1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡x-x+2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡x-x+2}}[{\int }_{-4/x}^{-1}\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡x-x+2}}\cdot y\,{|}_{-4/x}^{-1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}(\frac{4}{x}-1)\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡x-x+2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡x-x+2}\,{|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =2\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡4-4+2}-2\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡1-1+2} \\  & =2\sqrt{4\operatorname{ln}⁡4-2}-2 \\  & =2(\sqrt{8\operatorname{ln}⁡2-2}-1)\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-acad3c64-a048-5588-ba2a-180649362504"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $$

Now, this equation is pretty easy to solve. Because the bases on both sides of the equation are the same (they are both equal to $3$), we can simply equate the powers.

$$

$$

Therefore, the solution to this equation is $x=4.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186070029 :tutorial/content "Let's take a look at the following equation: 

$$

$$

We can't solve this equation straight off the bat because the two sides of the equation don't share a common base.

However, notice that $25$ can be written as a power of $5\mathbin{:}$

$$
25=5^2
$$

Therefore, we can rewrite the equation as

$$
5^x = 5^2.
$$

Since both sides of the equation are now written as an exponential expression with a common base of $5,$ we can set the exponents equal to each other and solve:

$$
\begin{aligned}{5}^{x} & ={5}^{2} \\ x & =2\end{aligned}
$$

To check that the solution is correct, we plug $x=2$ into the original equation:

$$
\eqalign{

17592186088394 :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
{y}^{″}+2{y}^{′}+y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +1 & =0 \\ {(\lambda +1)}^{2} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =-1$ is a repeated root, and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}=A{e}^{-x}+Bx{e}^{-x}
$$

We now need to find the particular solution${y}_{p}(x).$

The right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is $-25\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.$ Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡2x,
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x} & =-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡2x+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡2x \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =-4\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡2x-4\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡2x\end{aligned}
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
(-4\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡2x-4\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡2x)+2(-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡2x+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡2x)+(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡2x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡2x)=-25\operatorname{sin}⁡2x
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
(-3\alpha +4\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+(-4\alpha -3\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡2x=-25\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}-3\alpha +4\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡2x) \\ -4\alpha -3\beta =-25\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡2x)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =4$ and $\beta =3.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+3\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y=A{e}^{-x}+Bx{e}^{-x}+4\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+3\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.
$$

Now let us find constants $A$ and $B.$ 

Substituting $y(0)=4$ into the general solution gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}A+4 & =4 \\ A & =0\end{aligned}
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=0.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}:$

$$
{y}^{′}=-A{e}^{-x}+B{e}^{-x}-Bx{e}^{-x}-8\operatorname{sin}⁡2x+6\operatorname{cos}⁡2x
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ into the above gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}-A+B+6 & =0 \\ B & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $A=0,B=-6.$

So, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=-6x{e}^{-x}+4\operatorname{cos}⁡2x+3\operatorname{sin}⁡2x.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186087780 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-b54ddcc0-5401-5d92-820d-ec32389dd88e"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186404440 :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}+16y=0.
$$

Writing down and solving the auxiliary equation gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-16\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =\pm 4\text{i}$, and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=P\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡4x.
$$

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

The particular solution of the inhomogeneous equation cannot be of the form $\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡4x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡4x$ because this is already included in the complementary function. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form 

$$
{y}_{p}=x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡4x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡4x),
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x} & =(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡4x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡4x)+4x(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡4x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡4x) \\ \frac{{\text{d}}^{2}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =8(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡4x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡4x)+16x(-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡4x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡4x).\end{aligned}
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
8(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡4x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡4x)+16x(-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡4x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡4x)+16x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡4x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡4x)\,=4\operatorname{sin}⁡4x.
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
-8\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡4x+8\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡4x=4\operatorname{sin}⁡4x.
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡4x) \\ -8\alpha =4\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡4x)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{1}{2}$, $\beta =0.$
Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=-\frac{1}{2}x\operatorname{cos}⁡4x.
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y={y}_{c}+{y}_{p}=P\operatorname{cos}⁡4x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡4x-\frac{1}{2}x\operatorname{cos}⁡4x.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186088225 :question/worked-solution "First, we need to find the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x),$ which is the solution to the homogeneous equation

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+9 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-9\end{aligned}
$$

So $\lambda =\pm 3\text{i},$ and therefore the complementary function ${y}_{c}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{c}(x)=P\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡3x.
$$

We now need to find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x).$

The particular solution of the inhomogeneous equation cannot be of the form $\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡3x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡3x$ because this is already included in the complementary function. Therefore, we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡3x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡3x),
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined. 

Calculating the first and second derivatives of ${y}_{p}$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡3x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡3x)+3x(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡3x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡3x) \\ {y}^{″} & =6(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡3x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡3x)+9x(-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡3x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡3x).\end{aligned}
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute the derivatives into the differential equation:

$$
6(-\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡3x+\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡3x)+9x(-\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡3x-\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡3x)+9x(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡3x+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡3x)=6\operatorname{cos}⁡3x-12\operatorname{sin}⁡3x
$$

Grouping the terms on the left-hand side gives

$$
-6\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡3x+6\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡3x=6\operatorname{cos}⁡3x-12\operatorname{sin}⁡3x.
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\begin{aligned}\{\begin{aligned}6\beta =6\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡3x) \\ -6\alpha =-12\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡3x)\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =2,\beta =1.$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=x(2\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+\operatorname{sin}⁡3x).
$$

The general solution is given by

$$
y(x)={y}_{c}(x)+{y}_{p}(x),
$$

and therefore, the general solution in our case is

$$
y=P\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+Q\operatorname{sin}⁡3x+x(2\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+\operatorname{sin}⁡3x).
$$

Now let us find constants $P$ and $Q.$ 

Substituting $y(0)=2$ into the general solution gives

$$
P=2.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(0)=5.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}$:

$$
{y}^{′}=-3P\operatorname{sin}⁡3x+3Q\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+\operatorname{sin}⁡3x)+x(-6\operatorname{sin}⁡3x+3\operatorname{cos}⁡3x)
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(0)=5$ into the above gives

$$
3Q+2=5.
$$

Therefore, $P=2,Q=1.$

So, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y=2\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+\operatorname{sin}⁡3x+2x\operatorname{cos}⁡3x+x\operatorname{sin}⁡3x.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-b54ddcc0-5401-5d92-820d-ec32389dd88e" :question/id #uuid "b54ddcc0-5401-5d92-820d-ec32389dd88e" :question/math-academy-id "q-93821" :question/problem "Given that the differential equation

:question/problem "Solve the equation $2 = wz - 2w +1$ for the variable $w.$" :question/worked-solution "We need to isolate all terms with $w$ on one side of the equation. To do this, we subtract $1$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =wz-2w+1 \\ 2-1 & =wz-2w+1-1 \\ 1 & =wz-2w\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we factor out $w$ in the expression on the right-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =wz-2w \\ 1 & =w(z-2)\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide both sides by $(z-2)$ to isolate $w\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =w(z-2) \\ \frac{1}{z-2} & =\frac{w(z-2)}{z-2} \\ \frac{1}{z-2} & =\frac{w\cancel{(z-2)}}{\cancel{z-2}} \\ \frac{1}{z-2} & =w \\ w & =\frac{1}{z-2}\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** This result assumes that $z-2\neq 0.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186179640 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-03f30d76-6e4b-58e9-917f-05e941931839" "question-d1bde4eb-16c8-5f7c-8125-caf4a9cb1949"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186179469 :question/problem "Solve the equation $4ky=5y + 1$ for the variable $y.$" :question/worked-solution "We need to isolate all terms with $y$ on one side of the equation. To do this, we subtract $5y$ from both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}4ky & =5y+1 \\ 4ky-5y & =5y+1-5y \\ 4ky-5y & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that all terms containing $y$ are on the left-hand side, and all terms independent of $y$ are on the right-hand side.

Next, we factor out $y$ in the expression on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}4ky-5y & =1 \\ y(4k-5) & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide both sides by $(4k -5)$ to isolate $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(4k-5) & =1 \\ \frac{y(4k-5)}{(4k-5)} & =\frac{1}{(4k-5)} \\ \frac{y\cancel{(4k-5)}}{\cancel{(4k-5)}} & =\frac{1}{4k-5} \\ y & =\frac{1}{4k-5}\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** This result assumes that $4k-5\neq 0.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186179641 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-77fe19c1-2d2e-5ba1-9d49-d82b50f369df" "question-5eedbb0b-2f52-5239-8343-cadc5e74eba1"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186179471 :question/problem "Solve the equation $\dfrac{xy}{3} = \dfrac{y - 1}{2}$ for the variable $y.$" :question/worked-solution "We need to isolate all terms with $y$ on one side of the equation. To do this, we first cross-multiply:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{xy}{3} & =\frac{y-1}{2} \\ 2\cdot xy & =3\cdot (y-1) \\ 2xy & =3y-3\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we subtract $3y$ from both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}2xy & =3y-3 \\ 2xy-3y & =3y-3-3y \\ 2xy-3y & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that all terms containing $y$ are on the left-hand side, and all terms independent of $y$ are on the right-hand side.

Then, we factor out $y$ from the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}2xy-3y & =-3 \\ y(2x-3) & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide both sides by $(2x - 3)$ to isolate $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}y(2x-3) & =-3 \\ \frac{y(2x-3)}{2x-3} & =\frac{-3}{2x-3} \\ \frac{y\cancel{(2x-3)}}{\cancel{2x-3}} & =\frac{-3}{2x-3} \\ y & =-\frac{3}{2x-3}\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** This result assumes that $2x-3\neq 0.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-6b9f4cd9-9a85-5f2d-9eac-f617eac7ba39" :question/id #uuid "6b9f4cd9-9a85-5f2d-9eac-f617eac7ba39" :question/math-academy-id "q-133790" :question/problem "If $10=3rs+2s-2,$ then $s=$" :question/worked-solution "We need to isolate all terms with $s$ on one side of the equation. To do this, we add $2$ to both sides:

$$
\begin{aligned}10 & =3rs+2s-2 \\ 10+2 & =3rs+2s-2+2 \\ 12 & =3rs+2s\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we factor out $s$ in the expression on the right-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}12 & =3rs+2s \\ 12 & =s(3r+2)\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide both sides by $(3r+2)$ to isolate $s:$

$$
\begin{aligned}12 & =s(3r+2) \\ \frac{12}{3r+2} & =\frac{s(3r+2)}{3r+2} \\ \frac{12}{3r+2} & =\frac{s\cancel{(3r+2)}}{\cancel{3r+2}} \\ \frac{12}{3r+2} & =s \\ s & =\frac{12}{3r+2}\end{aligned}
$$

:question/math-academy-id "q-215778" :question/problem "If $7pq+1=3q+8,$ then $q=${{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "We need to isolate all terms with $q$ on one side of the equation. To do this, we start by subtracting $1$ from both sides: 

$$
\begin{aligned}7pq+1 & =3q+8 \\ 7pq+1-1 & =3q+8-1 \\ 7pq & =3q+7\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we subtract $3q$ from both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}7pq & =3q+7 \\ 7pq-3q & =3q+7-3q \\ 7pq-3q & =7\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that all terms containing $q$ are on the left-hand side, and all terms independent of $q$ are on the right-hand side.

Next, we factor out $q$ in the expression on the left-hand side.

$$
\begin{aligned}7pq-3q & =7 \\ (7p-3)q & =7\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide both sides by $(7p-3)$ to isolate $q:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(7p-3)q & =7 \\ \frac{(7p-3)q}{7p-3} & =\frac{7}{7p-3} \\ \frac{\cancel{(7p-3)}q}{\cancel{7p-3}} & =\frac{7}{7p-3} \\ q & =\frac{7}{7p-3}\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** This result assumes that $7p-3\ne 0.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-5be6f4c4-2cc2-5d19-b848-3c7a94a8c33e"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-5be6f4c4-2cc2-5d19-b848-3c7a94a8c33e" :answer-field/id #uuid "5be6f4c4-2cc2-5d19-b848-3c7a94a8c33e" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-6422d58b-a6aa-55ce-9272-f106d09fe53e" :answer-field/choices ["answer-6422d58b-a6aa-55ce-9272-f106d09fe53e"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-6422d58b-a6aa-55ce-9272-f106d09fe53e" :answer/id #uuid "6422d58b-a6aa-55ce-9272-f106d09fe53e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{7}{7p-3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-d1bde4eb-16c8-5f7c-8125-caf4a9cb1949" :question/id #uuid "d1bde4eb-16c8-5f7c-8125-caf4a9cb1949" :question/math-academy-id "q-45310" :question/problem "If $4c+5=3yc-2,$ then $c=$" :question/worked-solution "We need to isolate all terms with $c$ on one side of the equation. "77fe19c1-2d2e-5ba1-9d49-d82b50f369df" :question/math-academy-id "q-215810" :question/problem "If $\frac{7mn+2n}{4}=\frac{3m}{7},$ then $m=${{field-1}}." :question/worked-solution "We need to isolate all terms with $m$ on one side of the equation. To do this, we first cross-multiply:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{7mn+2n}{4} & =\frac{3m}{7} \\ 7\cdot (7mn+2n) & =4\cdot 3m \\ 49mn+14n & =12m\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we subtract $49mn$ from both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}49mn+14n & =12m \\ 49mn+14n-49mn & =12m-49mn \\ 14n & =12m-49mn\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that all terms containing $m$ are on the right-hand side, and all terms independent of $m$ are on the left-hand side.

Then, we factor out $m$ from the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}14n & =12m-49mn \\ 14n & =(12-49n)m\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide both sides by $(12-49n)$ to isolate $m:$

$$
\begin{aligned}14n & =(12-49n)m \\ \frac{14n}{12-49n} & =\frac{\cancel{(12-49n)}m}{\cancel{12-49n}} \\ \frac{14n}{12-49n} & =m \\ m & =\frac{14n}{12-49n}\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** This result assumes that $12-49n\ne 0.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-f4f33662-8742-5543-9baf-920fd7c6b4a9"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-f4f33662-8742-5543-9baf-920fd7c6b4a9" :answer-field/id #uuid "f4f33662-8742-5543-9baf-920fd7c6b4a9" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-5a03a7cf-903f-54d3-b7e5-bf17f2b1ce2c" :answer-field/choices ["answer-5a03a7cf-903f-54d3-b7e5-bf17f2b1ce2c"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-5a03a7cf-903f-54d3-b7e5-bf17f2b1ce2c" :answer/id #uuid "5a03a7cf-903f-54d3-b7e5-bf17f2b1ce2c" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{14n}{12-49n}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-5eedbb0b-2f52-5239-8343-cadc5e74eba1" :question/id #uuid "5eedbb0b-2f52-5239-8343-cadc5e74eba1" :question/math-academy-id "q-133899" :question/problem "If $\frac{2km}{3}=\frac{k+m}{5},$ then $k=$" :question/worked-solution "We need to isolate all terms with $k$ on one side of the equation. To do this, we first cross-multiply:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2km}{3} & =\frac{k+m}{5} \\ 5\cdot 2km & =3\cdot (k+m) \\ 10km & =3k+3m\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we subtract $3k$ from both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}10km & =3k+3m \\ 10km-3k & =3k+3m-3k \\ 10km-3k & =3m\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that all terms containing $k$ are on the left-hand side, and all terms independent of $k$ are on the right-hand side.

Then, we factor out $k$ from the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}10km-3k & =3m \\ k(10m-3) & =3m\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide both sides by $(10m-3)$ to isolate $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}k(10m-3) & =3m \\ \frac{k\cancel{(10m-3)}}{\cancel{10m-3}} & =\frac{3m}{10m-3} \\ k & =\frac{3m}{10m-3}\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** This result assumes that $10m-3\ne 0.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-e91e9fc2-d906-5396-a41f-f01e1ee236be"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-e91e9fc2-d906-5396-a41f-f01e1ee236be" :answer-field/id #uuid "e91e9fc2-d906-5396-a41f-f01e1ee236be" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-8ce32e74-d9b3-58fa-998a-893bfc6268a9" :answer-field/choices ["answer-24e0251b-e7d9-5216-b40b-a0569fb7444b" "answer-86b91cce-eb4e-5100-836e-cdaa979bba83" "answer-feb11450-ea29-5663-bed0-4e4bfd0d07bb" "answer-d8884393-a5fe-5722-81d1-f68055378b9d" "answer-8ce32e74-d9b3-58fa-998a-893bfc6268a9"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-24e0251b-e7d9-5216-b40b-a0569fb7444b" :answer/id #uuid "24e0251b-e7d9-5216-b40b-a0569fb7444b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{10m}{3m+3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-86b91cce-eb4e-5100-836e-cdaa979bba83" :answer/id #uuid "86b91cce-eb4e-5100-836e-cdaa979bba83" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{10m}{3m-3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-feb11450-ea29-5663-bed0-4e4bfd0d07bb" :answer/id #uuid "feb11450-ea29-5663-bed0-4e4bfd0d07bb" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3m-3}{10m}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-d8884393-a5fe-5722-81d1-f68055378b9d" :answer/id #uuid "d8884393-a5fe-5722-81d1-f68055378b9d" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3m}{10m+3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8ce32e74-d9b3-58fa-998a-893bfc6268a9" :answer/id #uuid "8ce32e74-d9b3-58fa-998a-893bfc6268a9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{3m}{10m-3}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186180781 :tutorial/content "When solving a multivariable equation for a particular variable, we sometimes have to factor some terms in the equation to reach the solution.

For example, let's solve the following equation for the variable $d\mathbin{:}$

$$
2cd - 3d = 5
$$

First, we factor out $d$ in the expression on the left-hand side. This gives

$$
d(2c-3) = 5.
$$

Then, we divide both sides of the equation by $(2c-3)$ to isolate $d\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}d(2c-3) & =5 \\ \frac{d(2c-3)}{2c-3} & =\frac{5}{2c-3} \\ \frac{d\cancel{(2c-3)}}{\cancel{2c-3}} & =\frac{5}{2c-3} \\ d & =\frac{5}{2c-3}\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** This result assumes that $2c-3\neq 0.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186179895 :activity/expected-seconds 660.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186180332 :step/math-academy-id 952850 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186180333 :step/math-academy-id 952851 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186180334 :step/math-academy-id 952855 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186180335 :step/math-academy-id 952859 :db/ensure [:step/validate]} {:db/id 17592186175983 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-6beef5a1-8cca-5685-897f-0ef5f4dc810f" "question-19e48035-430d-58ef-92e6-a92cd0b0c10e"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-6beef5a1-8cca-5685-897f-0ef5f4dc810f" :question/id #uuid "6beef5a1-8cca-5685-897f-0ef5f4dc810f" :question/math-academy-id "q-108772" :question/problem "Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=4{x}^{2}+8xy+4{y}^{2}.
$$

The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
\operatorname{arctan}⁡(g(x,y))=2x+C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =4(x+y)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & =4{z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=4{z}^{2}+1.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4{z}^{2}+1}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int \frac{1}{4{z}^{2}+1}\,\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2z) & =x+K \\ \operatorname{arctan}⁡(2z) & =2x+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=2K.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\operatorname{arctan}⁡(2x+2y)=2x+C
$$

Therefore, 

$$
g(x,y)=2x+2y.

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2+4{x}^{2}-4xy+{y}^{2}.
$$

The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=x+C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we factor the right-hand side of the given equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2+(2x-y)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z=2x-y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2-\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =2+{z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}={z}^{2}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ -\int \frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ \frac{1}{z} & =x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\frac{1}{2x-y}=x+C
$$

Therefore, 

$$
g(x,y)=\frac{1}{2x-y}.
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-bc2debc3-d327-56e2-a61e-77f8bfd4b277"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-bc2debc3-d327-56e2-a61e-77f8bfd4b277" :answer-field/id #uuid "bc2debc3-d327-56e2-a61e-77f8bfd4b277" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-4f23b489-a7f5-50dd-bb19-7df5255ff600" :answer-field/choices ["answer-79433229-f545-56b5-886f-fc91ab9ed976" "answer-32b7eb7e-d784-51cc-a6f7-a2687a072eb0" "answer-41220c31-7cbf-5328-9208-6b8aa44a20f9" "answer-4f23b489-a7f5-50dd-bb19-7df5255ff600" "answer-066638b5-b947-5188-95a4-7fb8fa301ba9"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-79433229-f545-56b5-886f-fc91ab9ed976" :answer/id #uuid "79433229-f545-56b5-886f-fc91ab9ed976" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "2x-y+1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-32b7eb7e-d784-51cc-a6f7-a2687a072eb0" :answer/id #uuid "32b7eb7e-d784-51cc-a6f7-a2687a072eb0" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{(2x-y)^{2}-1}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-41220c31-7cbf-5328-9208-6b8aa44a20f9" :answer/id #uuid "41220c31-7cbf-5328-9208-6b8aa44a20f9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{(2x-y)^{2}}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-4f23b489-a7f5-50dd-bb19-7df5255ff600" :answer/id #uuid "4f23b489-a7f5-50dd-bb19-7df5255ff600" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{1}{2x-y}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-066638b5-b947-5188-95a4-7fb8fa301ba9" :answer/id #uuid "066638b5-b947-5188-95a4-7fb8fa301ba9" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\frac{2}{x-y}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186177006 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we're given a differential equation of the form

$$
y' = F(x,y).
$$

By factoring the function $F(x,y),$ we can often convert this differential equation to one that is of the form 

$$
y' = f ( a x + b y ),
$$

where $a$ and $b$ are real constants. Then, using the substitution $z= ax+by,$ we can convert the equation to a separable differential equation. 

To illustrate, let's consider the differential equation

$$
y'  = 9x^2 - 6xy + y^2.
$$

Notice that the right-hand side is a perfect square. So, we factor it as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}=(3x-y)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z = 3x - y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} = 3 - \,\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} 
\quad \Rightarrow\quad 
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = 3 - \,\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}
$$

Therefore, we can write our equation in terms of $z$ as

$$
3 - \,\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} = z^2,
$$

which simplifies to

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}   = 3-z^2.
$$

We now have a separable differential equation." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186176146 :activity/expected-seconds 660.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} {:db/id 17592186096657 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-20bd28d6-3021-5539-a5f9-9ec2d307a221"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186096390 :question/problem "If $f(x) = 12 \cdot 2^{x},$ then $f(-4)=$" :question/worked-solution "To calculate $f(-4),$ we substitute $x=-4$ into the expression for $f(x).$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-4) & =12\cdot {2}^{-4} \\  & =12\cdot \frac{1}{{2}^{4}} \\  & =12\cdot \frac{1}{16} \\  & =\frac{12}{16} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186096658 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-169115e9-c4da-5b2d-98db-fdbf90bfcfbf" "question-b0a1af6d-481b-5cb9-88d9-fa115158484b"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186096391 :question/worked-solution "To get the mass of the isotope after $3$ years, we evaluate the function at $t=3.$ Substituting $t=3$ into the function $M(t)$ gives

\begin{aligned}M & =128{(\frac{1}{4})}^{t} \\  & =128{(\frac{1}{4})}^{3} \\  & =128\cdot \frac{{1}^{3}}{{4}^{3}} \\  & =128\cdot \frac{1}{64} \\  & =\frac{128}{64} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, after $3$ years, there will be $2$ grams of isotope remaining." :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186096659 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-d094ad0f-c26b-57d4-8a3d-3a131e61b0c8" "question-c97061a8-e888-5c8e-ae09-c8d25cf5d2a1"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186096392 :question/problem "Solve for $C$ given that $y(t) = C \cdot \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^{t}$ and $y(5)=1.$" :question/worked-solution "We substitute $t=5$ and $y(t)=1$ into the expression for $y(t),$ and get

Therefore, $C=32.$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186096660 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-a6431deb-d4ee-50b8-b78e-d09da4574bf6" "question-f6033ad1-0d99-515b-be18-2f73585eb731"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186096393 :question/problem "Given that $P(x) = 2 \cdot 5^{3x},$ find $x$ such that $P(x)=250.$" :question/worked-solution "First we substitute $P(x)=250$ into the equation:

$$

$$

$$

Finally, we solve for $x,$ using the fact that $125$ is a power of $5\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{5}^{3x} & ={5}^{3} \\ 3x & =3 \\ x & =1\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "question-20bd28d6-3021-5539-a5f9-9ec2d307a221" :question/id #uuid "20bd28d6-3021-5539-a5f9-9ec2d307a221" :question/math-academy-id "q-61716" :question/problem "If $h(t)=128\cdot {(\frac{1}{4})}^{t},$ then $h(3)=$" :question/worked-solution "To calculate $h(3),$ we substitute $t=3$ into the expression for $h(t).$ This gives

$$
5\cdot {4}^{t}=80
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5\cdot {4}^{t}}{5} & =\frac{80}{5} \\ \frac{\cancel{5}\cdot {4}^{t}}{\cancel{5}} & =16 \\ {4}^{t} & =16\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{4}^{t} & ={4}^{2} \\ t & =2\end{aligned}

{{field-1}}" :question/worked-solution "First, we substitute $h(t)=320$ into the equation:

$$
5\cdot {4}^{3t+6}=320
$$

We can divide both sides of the equation by the constant factor of $5:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5\cdot {4}^{3t+6}}{5} & =\frac{320}{5} \\ \frac{\cancel{5}\cdot {4}^{3t+6}}{\cancel{5}} & =64 \\ {4}^{3t+6} & =64\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we solve for $t$ using the fact that $64$ is a power of $4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{4}^{3t+6} & ={4}^{3} \\ 3t+6 & =3 \\ 3t & =-3 \\ t & =-1\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-aaa84f9b-eb74-5ae9-9fee-178d468d3d0a"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-aaa84f9b-eb74-5ae9-9fee-178d468d3d0a" :answer-field/id #uuid "aaa84f9b-eb74-5ae9-9fee-178d468d3d0a" :answer-field/key "field-1" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank :answer-field/correct "answer-649ad70b-e688-5d26-97db-4e5143cbf659" :answer-field/choices ["answer-649ad70b-e688-5d26-97db-4e5143cbf659"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-649ad70b-e688-5d26-97db-4e5143cbf659" :answer/id #uuid "649ad70b-e688-5d26-97db-4e5143cbf659" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "-1" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186097924 :tutorial/content "An **exponential function** is a function where a variable is contained within an exponent. For example, the function below is an exponential function:

$$
f(x) = 3^x
$$

Just like any other function, we can evaluate it for some particular value of $x,$ say at $x={\color{blue}{4}},$ by substituting this value of $x$ into the function:

$$
f(4) = 3^{\color{blue}{4}} = 81
$$

Another example of an exponential function is $g(x)$ below:

$$
g(x) = 16\cdot \left(\dfrac 1 2\right)^x
$$

We can evaluate this function at $x={\color{blue}{4}}$ using the power of quotient rule, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}g(4) & =16\cdot {(\frac{1}{2})}^{4} \\  & =16\cdot \frac{{1}^{4}}{{2}^{4}} \\  & =16\cdot \frac{1}{16} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Exponential functions are of huge practical importance in science, engineering, economics, and many other disciplines. Let's practice evaluating them." :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186097925 :tutorial/content "Suppose that we're given the following exponential function:

$$
f(t) = C\cdot 4^t
$$

In addition, we're told that $f(3) = 128.$ Can we use this information to find the unknown constant $C?$

To solve this problem, we substitute $t=3$ and $f(t) = 128$ and solve for $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}128 & =C\cdot {4}^{3} \\ 128 & =C\cdot 64 \\ \frac{128}{64} & =C \\ 2 & =C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $C=2.$ So our function expressed in full is

$$
f(t) = 2\cdot 4^t.
$$

We sometimes say that the **initial value** of the function is $2,$ because if we evaluate $f$ at $t=0,$ we get

$$
f(0) = 2\cdot 4^0 = 2\cdot 1 = 2.
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186097926 :tutorial/content "Let's consider the following exponential function:

$$
h(x) = 2^x
$$

Can we find the value of $x$ that gives $h(x)=64?$ Indeed, we can. To do this, we'll need to use our knowledge of exponential equations. 

First, we use the fact that $h(x)=64$ to write our equation as

$$
2^x = 64.
$$

This is an exponential equation. Since we know that $64$ is a power of $2,$ we can solve this equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{2}^{x} & =64 \\ {2}^{x} & ={2}^{6} \\ x & =6\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186096918 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]} [:db/retract 17592186284360 :answer-field/choices 17592186282900] "From the hyperboloid equation, we make $z$ the subject as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+4)^{2}+(y+3)^{2}-\frac{(z+5)^{2}}{16} & =-1 \\ (x+4)^{2}+(y+3)^{2}+1 & =\frac{(z+5)^{2}}{16}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(z+5)^{2}}{16} & =(x+4)^{2}+(y+3)^{2}+1 \\ (z+5)^{2} & =16((x+4)^{2}+(y+3)^{2}+1) \\ z+5 & =\pm 4\sqrt{(x+4)^{2}+(y+3)^{2}+1} \\ z & =-5\pm 4\sqrt{(x+4)^{2}+(y+3)^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

The square root is defined only for non-negative arguments. However, notice that for all $(x,y)\in {R}^{2},$ we have

$$
(x+4)^{2}+(y+3)^{2}+1\ge 0.
$$

Therefore, the domain of $z(x,y)$ is ${R}^{2}.$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-751f8b2e-9f8a-59f7-8b55-6cf5ae31cd83"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-751f8b2e-9f8a-59f7-8b55-6cf5ae31cd83" :answer-field/id #uuid "751f8b2e-9f8a-59f7-8b55-6cf5ae31cd83" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-3fcdf940-6360-5efc-815a-67685f2bcd39" :answer-field/choices ["answer-c13ff75f-ea2e-5e78-b3fd-6dfe315f448e" "answer-ad54fb20-d344-5be0-b621-c08138a7d222" "answer-c00ed966-6006-5b17-8212-cacd1e467d5b" "answer-8d2dd945-a79f-5959-bfa8-cdfafd1ac3cd" "answer-3fcdf940-6360-5efc-815a-67685f2bcd39"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c13ff75f-ea2e-5e78-b3fd-6dfe315f448e" :answer/id #uuid "c13ff75f-ea2e-5e78-b3fd-6dfe315f448e" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,(x+4)^{2}+(y+3)^{2}<1\}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-ad54fb20-d344-5be0-b621-c08138a7d222" :answer/id #uuid "ad54fb20-d344-5be0-b621-c08138a7d222" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,(x+4)^{2}+(y+3)^{2}>1\}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c00ed966-6006-5b17-8212-cacd1e467d5b" :answer/id #uuid "c00ed966-6006-5b17-8212-cacd1e467d5b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,(x+4)^{2}+(y+3)^{2}\ge 1\}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-8d2dd945-a79f-5959-bfa8-cdfafd1ac3cd" :answer/id #uuid "8d2dd945-a79f-5959-bfa8-cdfafd1ac3cd" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,(x+4)^{2}+(y+3)^{2}\le 1\}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-3fcdf940-6360-5efc-815a-67685f2bcd39" :answer/id #uuid "3fcdf940-6360-5efc-815a-67685f2bcd39" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "{R}^{2}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186284469 :question/worked-solution "From the hyperboloid equation, we make $z$ the subject as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+5)^{2}+{y}^{2}-(z-3)^{2} & =1 \\ (x+5)^{2}+{y}^{2}-1 & =(z-3)^{2}\end{aligned}

$$

Since the square root is defined only for non-negative arguments, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+5)^{2}+{y}^{2}-1 & \ge 0 \\ (x+5)^{2}+{y}^{2} & \ge 1,\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the exterior of the circle $(x+5)^{2}+{y}^{2}=1,$ which includes the boundary.

Therefore, the domain is

$$
\{(x,y)\,:\,(x+5)^{2}+{y}^{2}\ge 1\}.
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186283953 :answer-field/correct "answer-639e7663-1b18-512b-aaa1-be4700f6151a" :answer-field/choices ["answer-c59c6bc5-e7d5-524f-b87d-e788fbdad7bc" "answer-389cbac5-a671-5c39-a922-51617d9c06fe" "answer-639e7663-1b18-512b-aaa1-be4700f6151a" "answer-36789465-716b-57b5-bcb5-c61d70e72a4f"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c59c6bc5-e7d5-524f-b87d-e788fbdad7bc" :answer/id #uuid "c59c6bc5-e7d5-524f-b87d-e788fbdad7bc" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,(x+5)^{2}+{y}^{2}<3\}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-389cbac5-a671-5c39-a922-51617d9c06fe" :answer/id #uuid "389cbac5-a671-5c39-a922-51617d9c06fe" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,(x+5)^{2}+{y}^{2}>1\}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-639e7663-1b18-512b-aaa1-be4700f6151a" :answer/id #uuid "639e7663-1b18-512b-aaa1-be4700f6151a" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,(x+5)^{2}+{y}^{2}\ge 1\}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-36789465-716b-57b5-bcb5-c61d70e72a4f" :answer/id #uuid "36789465-716b-57b5-bcb5-c61d70e72a4f" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "\{(x,y)\,:\,(x+5)^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 3\}" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "question-cfd858a6-a00f-5a94-8347-c41608b62519" :question/id #uuid "cfd858a6-a00f-5a94-8347-c41608b62519" :question/math-academy-id "q-164375" :question/problem "What is the trace in the $xz$-plane of the hyperboloid of two sheets $-\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=-1?$" :question/worked-solution "To find the trace in the $xz$-plane, we substitute $y=0$ into the equation of the hyperboloid. | $\quad x \quad$ | $5$ | $6$ | $7$ | $8$ | $9$ | $10$ | $11$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $P(X\leq x)$ | $\,0.1157\,$ | $\,0.2068\,$ | $\,0.3239\,$ | $\,\,\,\,\,\,?\,\,\,\,\,\,$ | $\,0.5874\,$ | $\,0.7060\,$ | $\,0.8030\,$ |" :question/worked-solution "The cumulative distribution function of a discrete random variable $X$ is a function $F(x)$ such that

$$
F(x) = P(X \leq x).
$$

The probability mass function for the Poisson distribution $\textrm{Po}(\lambda)$ is given by

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{\lambda^x e^{-\lambda}}{x!}, \qquad x=0,1,2,3, \ldots\,.
$$

In our case, $\lambda=9.$ 

Therefore, we compute the missing element of the table as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(8) & =P(X\le 8) \\  & =P(X\le 7)+P(X=8) \\  & =F(7)+P(X=8) \\  & =0.3239+\frac{{9}^{8}\cdot {e}^{-9}}{8!} \\  & ≈0.4557\end{aligned}
$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166736 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-47d084d0-558c-55b5-8190-75e291aec240" "question-77a09fd4-a75e-503e-85e7-5369cc0e38f9" "question-88a38ed6-7fa9-5b5b-87c9-ffc4db1074d1" "question-6ed46a6a-33c2-5d2f-895f-2046417a88d9"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166499 :question/problem "Using the cumulative distribution function table of the Poisson random variable $X \sim \textrm{Po}(6)$ given below, compute $P(X=7).$

| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

$$
F(x) = P(X \leq x).
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(7) & =P(X\le 7) \\  & =P(X\in \{0,1,…,7\}) \\  & =P(X\in \{0,1,…,6\})+P(X=7) \\  & =P(X\le 6)+P(X=7) \\  & =F(6)+P(X=7).\end{aligned}

Therefore,

$$

$$" :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166737 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-bfd17aa5-30fb-5cb9-aef8-99d3d322cf8d" "question-a9431e7c-b663-534c-b1f2-e2cde30992c6" "question-d0dd1d6e-e305-5637-930e-c61c5f8b750e" "question-f97c8702-16dc-518f-875a-9b5c78750b8c" "question-3fd62c03-4c13-5eaa-a871-a2d0ae21b2c3"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id 17592186166500 :question/problem "Using the cumulative distribution function table of the Poisson random variable $X \sim \textrm{Po}(8)$ given below, compute $P(3 \leq X \leq 6).$

In this lesson, we'll learn how to construct CDF tables for the Poisson distribution and use them to calculate probabilities.

First, recall that the probability mass function of the Poisson distribution $\textrm{Po}(\lambda)$ is given by

$$
f(x) = \dfrac{\lambda^x e^{-\lambda}}{x!}, \qquad x=0,1,2,\ldots
$$

where $\lambda$ is a positive parameter.

The CDF of a discrete random variable $X$ is a function $F(x)$ such that

$$
F(x) = P(X \leq x).
$$

With that in mind, let's compute the values of $F(x)$ for the distribution $\textrm{Po}(2)$ at $x=0$ and $x=1.$  

To do that, we use the definition of the cumulative distribution function:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(0) & =P(X\le 0) \\  & =P(X=0) \\  & =\frac{{2}^{0}\cdot {e}^{-2}}{0!} \\  & =\frac{1\cdot {e}^{-2}}{1} \\  & ≈0.1353 \\ F(1) & =P(X\le 1) \\  & =P(X=0)+P(X=1) \\  & =\frac{{2}^{0}\cdot {e}^{-2}}{0!}+\frac{{2}^{1}\cdot {e}^{-2}}{1!} \\  & =\frac{1\cdot {e}^{-2}}{1}+\frac{2\cdot {e}^{-2}}{1} \\  & ≈0.4060\end{aligned}
$$

The CDF data is usually presented as a table. If we were to continue this process and calculate $F(2), F(3), F(4),$ and $F(5),$ our table would look as follows:

| $\quad x \quad$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ | $5$ | $\cdots$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $P(X\leq x)$ | $\,0.1353\,$ | $\,0.4060\,$ | $\,0.6767\,$ | $\,0.8571\,$ | $\,0.9473\,$ | $\,0.9834\,$ | $\,\,\,\cdots\,\,\,$ |

Note the following:

- $F(x)$ is an increasing function.

- Since $\textrm{Po}(\lambda)$ takes arbitrarily large values, we have $F(x) < 1$ for all $n,$ and $F(x) \to 1$ as $x\to\infty.$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186167037 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}] "assertions" [[17592186110320 :question/problem "Solve the equation $\dfrac{2x+5}{30} = \dfrac{1}{2}.$"] [17592186110320 :question/worked-solution "First, we cross-multiply:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2x+5}{30} & =\frac{1}{2} \\ (2x+5)\cdot 2 & =30\cdot 1\end{aligned}

$$"] [17592186110321 :question/problem "Solve for $x$, where $\dfrac{6-2x}{2} = \dfrac{6-x}{3}.$"] [17592186110321 :question/worked-solution "First, we cross-multiply:

Then, we proceed as usual to solve the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}(6-2x)\cdot 3 & =2\cdot (6-x) \\ 18-6x & =12-2x \\ 18-6x-18 & =12-2x-18 \\ -6x & =-2x-6 \\ -6x+2x & =-2x-6+2x \\ -4x & =-6 \\ \frac{-4x}{-4} & =\frac{-6}{-4} \\ x & =\frac{6}{4} \\ x & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186110322 :question/problem "Solve for $u$, where $\dfrac{u+2}{3} = - \dfrac{3-u}{2}.$"] [17592186110322 :question/worked-solution "We transfer the negative into the numerator of the fraction, and proceed with cross-multiplication:

So, we can write $A=PD{P}^{-1},$ where $P$ is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $A$ and $D$ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues in the corresponding order:

$$

$$

$$

:question/problem "Find a $2\times 2$ matrix $H$ that has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=7,$ and corresponding eigenvectors

$$

So, we can write $H=PD{P}^{-1},$ where $P$ is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $H,$ and $D$ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues in the corresponding order:

$$
H={{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Let $P=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}].$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-2 & -3 \\ -2 & -2\end{aligned}]=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, carrying out the necessary matrix multiplication, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}H & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{aligned}](\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}-4 & 21 \\ 4 & -14\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}17 & 15 \\ -10 & -8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

Compute ${f}_{Y|X}(2\,|\,3)$ given that the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ shown in the table above."] ["question-654ece2b-abda-569c-8738-da98c426c46e" :question/worked-solution "The conditional probability mass function ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)$ is defined as

$$
{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=P(Y=y\,|\,X=x).
$$

Therefore, we're required to compute the conditional probability

$$
{f}_{Y|X}(2\,|\,3)=P(Y=2\,|\,X=3).
$$

By the multiplication law for conditional probability, we have

$$
P(Y=2\,|\,X=3)=\frac{P(X=3,Y=2)}{P(X=3)}=\frac{f(3,2)}{{f}_{X}(3)}
$$

where $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability mass function of $X$ and $Y,$ and ${f}_{X}(x)$ is the marginal distribution of $X.$

Recall that the marginal distribution for $X$ corresponds to the row totals. Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(3) & =f(3,2)+f(3,4) \\  & =\frac{9}{20}+\frac{1}{20} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given table, $f(3,2)=\frac{9}{20}.$ 

Finally, substituting  ${f}_{X}(3)=\frac{1}{2}$ and $f(3,2)=\frac{9}{20}$ in our formula above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y|X}(2\,|\,3) & =P(Y=2\,|\,X=3) \\  & =\frac{f(3,2)}{{f}_{X}(3)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{9}{20})}{(\frac{1}{2})} \\  & =\frac{9}{10}.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-654ece2b-abda-569c-8738-da98c426c46e" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-d5318616-df05-5cb7-9c1a-585554d2944f" :answer-field/id #uuid "answer-field-d5318616-df05-5cb7-9c1a-585554d2944f"] [17592186162105 :knowledge-point/questions "question-654ece2b-abda-569c-8738-da98c426c46e"] [17592186244002 :question/problem "Consider the set of matrices $\{A,B,C\},$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}-3 & -1 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}4 & -4 \\ -8 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

 
If the set is linearly dependent, find the value of $\frac{{x}_{1}}{{x}_{2}}$ from a non-zero solution of ${x}_{1}A+{x}_{2}B+{x}_{3}C=O,$ where $O$ is the $2\times 2$ zero-matrix."] [17592186244002 :question/worked-solution "If the set is linearly dependent, then there exist ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3}$ not all zero such that 

$$
{x}_{1}A+{x}_{2}B+{x}_{3}C=O.
$$

Otherwise, if ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}=0,$ the set is linearly independent.

Substituting the matrices $A,$ $B,$ and $C$ into the above equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-3 & -1 \\ 2 & 4\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}4 & -4 \\ -8 & 0\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{1} \\ 0 & -2{x}_{1}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-3{x}_{2} & -{x}_{2} \\ 2{x}_{2} & 4{x}_{2}\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}4{x}_{3} & -4{x}_{3} \\ -8{x}_{3} & 0\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}+4{x}_{3} & {x}_{1}-{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3} \\ 2{x}_{2}-8{x}_{3} & -2{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding entries, we obtain the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}+4{x}_{3}=0 \\ {x}_{1}-{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3}=0 \\ 2{x}_{2}-8{x}_{3}=0 \\ -2{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we consider the corresponding augmented matrix and reduce it to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 4 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -8 & 0 \\ -2 & 4 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{4}:={R}_{4}+2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 8 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2} \\ {R}_{4}:={R}_{4}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & -8 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd.
Hence, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable.

The system is now

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}+4{x}_{3}=0 \\ 2{x}_{2}-8{x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

From the $2$nd equation, we get ${x}_{2}=4{x}_{3}.$ Substitute it into the first equation to get

$$
{x}_{1}-3(4{x}_{3})+4{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=8{x}_{3}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is 

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}8{x}_{3} \\ 4{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Finally, for any ${x}_{3}\ne 0,$ we obtain

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}}{{x}_{2}}=\frac{8{x}_{3}}{4{x}_{3}}=2.
$$"] [17592186247185 :question/worked-solution "In order to determine whether $b$ lies in $\text{Col}(C),$ we need to check if the equation $Cx=b$ is consistent. So, let's find the row echelon form of the augmented matrix $[C\,|\,b]$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[C\,|\,b] & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 9 \\ 3 & -3 & -15\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 9 \\ 0 & 0 & 12\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=9 \\ 0=12.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get the false statement $0=12.$  

Therefore, the system is inconsistent, which implies that $b\notin \text{Col}(C).$"] ["activity-bb01d4c0-3f68-5297-9f60-c8adea4b1367" :activity/id #uuid "bb01d4c0-3f68-5297-9f60-c8adea4b1367"] Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1},
$$

where ${P}_{B\to C}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$

First, let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ and $\{{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of vectors from $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ To do this, we consider the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

We reduce $M$ using Gaussian elimination until we get the identity matrix on the left. By doing this, we obtain the required change-of-coordinates matrix on the right.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 11 & 6 \\ -1 & 1 & -5 & -3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 11 & 6 \\ 0 & 3 & 6 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 11 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 7 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}7 & 4 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}7 & 4 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1\cdot 7-2\cdot 4}[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ -2 & 7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 \\ 2 & -7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C:$

:question/worked-solution "To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =3.$ So, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & 1 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 4 \\ 2 & -2 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+4{x}_{3}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}-4{x}_{3}=0 \\ 0=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 4 & 0 \\ 2 & -2 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are free variables. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}.$ So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2},{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Therefore, the required basis is

$$
B=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}.
$$"] ["answer-2509f728-ac88-5bed-b4bc-f65ab44a09f7" :answer/id #uuid "2509f728-ac88-5bed-b4bc-f65ab44a09f7"] ["answer-2509f728-ac88-5bed-b4bc-f65ab44a09f7" :answer/type :answer.type/math] $$

Consider the matrix $A$ shown above. What are the dimensions of the eigenspaces ${V}_{-3}$ and ${V}_{-1}$ corresponding to eigenvalues $\lambda =-3$ and $\lambda =-1$ of $A$, respectively?"] ["question-3be1ddbd-2595-5ba8-8ba6-f7f8cb00a8ea" :question/worked-solution "First, we write down the characteristic equation $\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{det}(A-\lambda I)=0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 5 & 1 \\ 0 & -3-\lambda  & 0 \\ -8 & -10 & -5-\lambda \end{aligned}|=0 \\ (-3-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & 1 \\ -8 & -5-\lambda \end{aligned}|=0 \\ (-3-\lambda )((1-\lambda )(-5-\lambda )+8)=0 \\ -(\lambda +3)({\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +3)=0 \\ (\lambda +3)(\lambda +3)(\lambda +1)=0 \\ (\lambda +3)^{2}(\lambda +1)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=-3$ (double root) and ${\lambda }_{3}=-1$ (simple root).

Let's now consider the eigenspaces corresponding to each eigenvector:

- First, we consider $\lambda =-1.$ Since ${V}_{-1}$ corresponds to a simple root, we obtain 

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{-1})=1.
$$

- Then, we consider $\lambda =-3,$ which is a repeated root of the characteristic equation. To find the dimension of ${V}_{-3},$ we row-reduce the matrix $(A-(-3)I)\text{x}=0:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 5 & 1 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ -8 & -10 & -5\end{aligned}]-(-3)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -8 & -10 & -2\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). This implies that we will have $3-1=2$ linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-3.$ Therefore, 

$$
\text{dim}({V}_{-3})=2.
$$"] ["question-3be1ddbd-2595-5ba8-8ba6-f7f8cb00a8ea" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-5c1f5525-34b9-510b-9cff-55fc25573d40" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
m\angle{A} + m\angle{B} + m\angle{C} = 180^\circ .

Then, we multiply both sides of the equation by $3\mathbin{:}$

{{field-1}}"] ["question-a062c0fa-ba5c-540d-bad1-e5dc2b1fdc72" :question/worked-solution "We need to isolate the variable $x.$ First, we cross-multiply:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2x+1}{3} & =\frac{y-x}{2} \\ 2\cdot (2x+1) & =3\cdot (y-x) \\ 4x+2 & =3y-3x\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we subtract $2$ to both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}4x+2 & =3y-3x \\ 4x+2-2 & =3y-3x-2 \\ 4x & =3y-3x-2\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we add $3x$ to both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}4x & =3y-3x-2 \\ 4x+3x & =3y-3x-2+3x \\ 7x & =3y-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide both sides of the equation by $7:$

$$
\begin{aligned}7x & =3y-2 \\ \frac{7x}{7} & =\frac{3y-2}{7} \\ \frac{\cancel{7}x}{\cancel{7}} & =\frac{3y-2}{7} \\ x & =\frac{3y-2}{7}\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-a062c0fa-ba5c-540d-bad1-e5dc2b1fdc72" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard] ["answer-field-c3558bc4-d6aa-5a60-9e85-1a7a6d4326f5" :answer-field/id #uuid "c3558bc4-d6aa-5a60-9e85-1a7a6d4326f5"] ["answer-541438b0-3d68-5da1-8797-bf586ce1dc59" :answer/id #uuid "541438b0-3d68-5da1-8797-bf586ce1dc59"] ["answer-541438b0-3d68-5da1-8797-bf586ce1dc59" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-541438b0-3d68-5da1-8797-bf586ce1dc59" :answer/value "\frac{3y-2}{7}"] ["answer-field-c3558bc4-d6aa-5a60-9e85-1a7a6d4326f5" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-c3558bc4-d6aa-5a60-9e85-1a7a6d4326f5" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-c3558bc4-d6aa-5a60-9e85-1a7a6d4326f5" :answer-field/correct "answer-541438b0-3d68-5da1-8797-bf586ce1dc59"] ["answer-field-c3558bc4-d6aa-5a60-9e85-1a7a6d4326f5" :answer-field/choices "answer-541438b0-3d68-5da1-8797-bf586ce1dc59"] ["question-a062c0fa-ba5c-540d-bad1-e5dc2b1fdc72" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-c3558bc4-d6aa-5a60-9e85-1a7a6d4326f5"] [17592186064349 :knowledge-point/questions "question-a062c0fa-ba5c-540d-bad1-e5dc2b1fdc72"] ["question-a390d02a-3ecf-5fc0-8eb1-0f04dc4eff6f" :question/id #uuid "a390d02a-3ecf-5fc0-8eb1-0f04dc4eff6f"] ["question-a390d02a-3ecf-5fc0-8eb1-0f04dc4eff6f" :question/math-academy-id "q-178606"] ["question-a390d02a-3ecf-5fc0-8eb1-0f04dc4eff6f" :question/problem "Given that $4x-y=7-5y,$ express $y$ in terms of $x.$

{{field-1}}"] ["question-a390d02a-3ecf-5fc0-8eb1-0f04dc4eff6f" :question/worked-solution "We need to isolate the variable $y.$ To do this, we treat $x$ as though it were a constant and apply the addition and multiplication principles as usual.

Then, we subtract $4x$ from both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}4x+4y & =7 \\ 4x+4y-4x & =7-4x \\ 4y & =7-4x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide both sides of the equation by $4:$

$$

{{field-1}}"] ["question-73aef377-5ed1-5df9-8acf-ea492a3b5fe7" :question/worked-solution "The infimum of a set $D$ is the greatest lower bound of $D.$

If $D$ is a finite set, the infimum of $D$ equals its minimum.

First, let's write down all the terms of our set by substituting $n=1,2,3,4$ into the expression for the elements of $D:$

$$
\begin{aligned}1-{1}^{2} & =0 \\ 2-{2}^{2} & =-2 \\ 3-{3}^{2} & =-6 \\ 4-{4}^{2} & =-12\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
D=\{0,\,-2,\,-6,\,-12\}.
$$

Therefore,

The infimum of $B$ is the {{field-1}} of $B,$ and the supremum is the {{field-2}} of $B.$

Since $B$ is {{field-5}}, we have $sup(B)$ {{field-6}}."] ["question-506b27d0-9ecb-54b1-8cb0-ba21f98fbff3" :question/worked-solution "The infimum of $B$ is the greatest lower bound of $B,$ and the supremum is the smallest upper bound of $B.$

To find the infimum of this set, we must find the set containing **all** lower bounds of $B$ (i.e., the set of lower bounds) and take the maximum of this set.

Since $B$ is unbounded below, $B$ has no lower bounds, so $inf(B)=-\infty .$

Next, to find the supremum of this set, we must find the set containing **all** upper bounds of $B$ (i.e., the set of upper bounds) and take the minimum of this set.

In our case, we have the following:

- Any number in the set $x\ge \sqrt{2}$ is greater than or equal to the elements of $B.$ Thus, the set $[\sqrt{2},\infty )$ contains only upper bounds of $B.$

- Any number in the set $x<\sqrt{2}$ is **not** an upper bound of $B.$ In other words, we can always find an element of $B$ that is greater than $x$ for any $x<\sqrt{2}.$

Therefore, $[\sqrt{2},\infty )$ is the set of upper bounds of $B,$ and

$$
sup(B)=min\,[\sqrt{2},\infty )=\sqrt{2}.
$$

The completed reasoning is given below.

The infimum of a set $B$ is the $\text{greatest lower bound}$ of $B,$ and the supremum is the $\text{smallest upper bound}$ of $B.$

Since $B$ is $\text{unbounded below},$ we have $inf(B)=-\infty .$

Since $B$ is $\text{bounded above},$ we have $sup(B)=\sqrt{2}.$"] ["question-506b27d0-9ecb-54b1-8cb0-ba21f98fbff3" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] To find the infimum of this set, we must find the set containing **all** lower bounds of $B$ (i.e., the set of lower bounds) and take the maximum of this set.

In our case, we have the following:

- Any number in the set $x\le -1$ is smaller than or equal to the elements of $B.$ Thus, the set $(-\infty ,-1]$ contains only lower bounds of $B.$

- Any number in the set $x>-1$ is **not** a lower bound of $B.$ In other words, we can always find an element of $B$ that is smaller than $x$ for any $x>-1.$

Therefore, $(-\infty ,-1]$ is the set of lower bounds of $B,$ and

$$
inf(B)=max(-\infty ,-1]=-1.
$$

Notice that $-1$ is also the minimum of $B.$

The completed reasoning is given below.

The infimum of $B$ is the $\text{greatest lower bound}$ of $B.$

The set of lower bounds of $B$ is as follows:

$$
\{x\in R\,:\,x\le -1\}
$$

Therefore, $inf(B)=-1\in B.$"] ["question-d48b0cc5-05e8-55c3-b441-64611554a8ed" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-7711e40c-c300-5c27-b9a0-b4edcb7004f6" :answer-field/id The elements of $A$ are the terms of the sequence ${a}_{n},$ given by

$$
{a}_{n}=1+3{(\frac{1}{4})}^{n},\,n\in N=\{1,2,3,4,…\}.
$$

Let's draw some points of our sequence on the real line:

![](images/19/198c3d6737439fcfa204926394b317aae0026502b5eaacb9e2f0429941f23db3.png)

We see that ${a}_{n}$ is decreasing and converges to $1.$ The maximum of $A$ is 

$$
max(A)={a}_{1}=1+3{(\frac{1}{4})}^{1}=\frac{7}{4}.
$$

So, in our case, we have that

- any number $x\ge {a}_{1}$ is an upper bound of $A,$

- any number $x<{a}_{1}$ cannot be an upper bound because ${a}_{1},$ an element of $A,$ is greater than $x.$

Therefore, $[\frac{7}{4},\infty )$ is the set of upper bounds of $A,$ and 

$$
sup(A)=min[\frac{7}{4},\infty )=\frac{7}{4}.
$$

Notice that $\frac{7}{4}$ is the maximum of $A.$ Therefore, we conclude that

$$
sup(A)=\frac{7}{4}\in A.
$$"] [17592186162530 :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-fdb9e03b-cb3d-5a8d-9ae0-14d4a6eba10a" :answer/id #uuid "fdb9e03b-cb3d-5a8d-9ae0-14d4a6eba10a"] ["answer-fdb9e03b-cb3d-5a8d-9ae0-14d4a6eba10a" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-fdb9e03b-cb3d-5a8d-9ae0-14d4a6eba10a" :answer/value "sup(A)=1\in A"] ["answer-7d320ab4-e7ea-5b1a-9b1e-fcd8c46760b7" :answer/id #uuid "7d320ab4-e7ea-5b1a-9b1e-fcd8c46760b7"] ["answer-7d320ab4-e7ea-5b1a-9b1e-fcd8c46760b7" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-7d320ab4-e7ea-5b1a-9b1e-fcd8c46760b7" :answer/value "sup(A)=1\notin A"] ["answer-128ee1a2-ad98-5075-846f-b8cbe5627a55" :answer/id #uuid "128ee1a2-ad98-5075-846f-b8cbe5627a55"] ["answer-128ee1a2-ad98-5075-846f-b8cbe5627a55" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-128ee1a2-ad98-5075-846f-b8cbe5627a55" :answer/value "sup(A)=\frac{7}{4}\in A"] ["answer-ec2c2649-8169-5a93-bf6e-55c2f61519ac" :answer/id #uuid "ec2c2649-8169-5a93-bf6e-55c2f61519ac"] ["answer-ec2c2649-8169-5a93-bf6e-55c2f61519ac" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-ec2c2649-8169-5a93-bf6e-55c2f61519ac" :answer/value "sup(A)=\frac{7}{4}\notin A"] [17592186160502 :answer-field/correct "answer-128ee1a2-ad98-5075-846f-b8cbe5627a55"] [17592186160502 :answer-field/choices "answer-fdb9e03b-cb3d-5a8d-9ae0-14d4a6eba10a"] [17592186160502 :answer-field/choices "answer-7d320ab4-e7ea-5b1a-9b1e-fcd8c46760b7"] [17592186160502 :answer-field/choices "answer-128ee1a2-ad98-5075-846f-b8cbe5627a55"] [17592186160502 :answer-field/choices "answer-ec2c2649-8169-5a93-bf6e-55c2f61519ac"] ["question-d021d0f6-fbf3-5eed-804d-eee551071be6" :question/id #uuid "d021d0f6-fbf3-5eed-804d-eee551071be6"] ["question-d021d0f6-fbf3-5eed-804d-eee551071be6" :question/math-academy-id "q-253911"] ["question-d021d0f6-fbf3-5eed-804d-eee551071be6" :question/problem "Consider the following set.

$$

To find the supremum of a set $A,$ we must find the set containing **all** upper bounds of $A$ (i.e., the set of upper bounds) and take the minimum of this set.

- any number $y<3$ cannot be an upper bound of $A$ because $3,$ an element of $A,$ is greater than $y.$

$$
{sup}_{x\in R}f(x)=sup(A)=min[3,\infty )=3.
$$"] ["question-ddf4ec2c-4f4d-56c1-bc14-78cfd2f52940" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/easy] ["answer-field-42f7eabb-2484-504e-a47e-b134986a6e92" :answer-field/id #uuid "42f7eabb-2484-504e-a47e-b134986a6e92"] ["answer-67197de5-74fe-5dc0-abe6-0952b996a82d" :answer/id #uuid "67197de5-74fe-5dc0-abe6-0952b996a82d"] ["answer-67197de5-74fe-5dc0-abe6-0952b996a82d" :answer/type :answer.type/math] ["answer-67197de5-74fe-5dc0-abe6-0952b996a82d" :answer/value "3"] ["answer-field-42f7eabb-2484-504e-a47e-b134986a6e92" :answer-field/key "field-1"] ["answer-field-42f7eabb-2484-504e-a47e-b134986a6e92" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/blank] ["answer-field-42f7eabb-2484-504e-a47e-b134986a6e92" :answer-field/correct "answer-67197de5-74fe-5dc0-abe6-0952b996a82d"] ["answer-field-42f7eabb-2484-504e-a47e-b134986a6e92" :answer-field/choices "answer-67197de5-74fe-5dc0-abe6-0952b996a82d"] ["question-ddf4ec2c-4f4d-56c1-bc14-78cfd2f52940" :question/answer-fields "answer-field-42f7eabb-2484-504e-a47e-b134986a6e92"] [17592186162159 :knowledge-point/questions "question-ddf4ec2c-4f4d-56c1-bc14-78cfd2f52940"] [17592186114982 :question/worked-solution "In the triangle we see two congruent sides,

classified by sides or by angles.

First, let's consider the classifications by sides. We have three groups of triangles:

- **Equilateral** triangles, where all sides have the same length.

- **Isosceles** triangles, where only two sides are congruent. The congruent sides are called the **legs** of the triangle, and the third side is called the **base**.

- **Scalene** triangles, where all sides have different measures.

![](images/dc/dc38034d6c202b5168fc8184511a839eb41af206eb733e71e5f5c2fa970c0e33.png)"] [17592186116447 :tutorial/content "Now, let's consider classifying triangles by angles. We have three groups of triangles.

- In an **acute** triangle, all three angles are acute.

- A triangle with a right angle is called a **right** triangle.

- A triangle with an obtuse angle is called an **obtuse** triangle.

![](images/f1/f1c28d1f4b1ec7a93f1778e63be3727aa227e8eea5320eb7d5579c697e709429.png)"] [17592186116448 :tutorial/content "Consider the following scalene triangle, where $AB=5$, $BC=7,$ and $AC=6$ units, respectively.

![](images/57/57be69075640f742ffe6c004515485c4f479347f3b8b523272778948935048df.png)

Looking at the angles, it's hard to tell which angle is the largest.

However, since we know the sides, there is a simple rule that we can use to determine the relative size of the angles:

Longer sides are opposite to larger angles and vice versa.

Applying this rule to $\triangle{ABC}$ depicted above, the longest side is $\overline{BC}.$ Therefore, the largest angle is the angle opposite to $\overline{BC},$ which is $\color{red}\angle{A}.$

![](images/82/82d9ac6d61f285f3557d2dd0dda826803ffae306c5f9a927a422b3b953f262f4.png)

Similarly,

- the mid-sized side ($\overline{AC}$) is opposite to the mid-sized angle ($\angle B$), and

- the shortest side ($\overline{AB}$) is opposite to the smallest angle ($\angle C$).

So, from least to greatest, the angles of the triangle are ordered as follows:

$$
m\angle{C} < m\angle{B} < m\angle{A}
$$

**Note:** This rule works in reverse too. If you know the biggest angle of a triangle, the longest side is always opposite to this angle."] [17592186115429 :activity/expected-seconds 540.0] [17592186171897 :question/problem "Which of the following regions are simply connected?

if every simple closed curve in $D$ can be contracted to a point.

![](images/46/46305c070e2563b4dacf8b31c88c46b860f003b20ffdff608a5485c09a91bd11.png)

A connected *plane* region $D$ is simply connected if every simple closed curve in $D$ encloses only points in $D.$ In other words, the region does not contain any holes. Plane regions containing holes are not simply connected, since some simple closed curves cannot be contracted to a point:

![](images/a0/a0459ddbabbd810e43db084f5dd174437340914b53ed227f6ef7ce2e3a0fc383.png)

$y.$"] [17592186179465 :question/worked-solution "We need to isolate $y.$ To do this, we first add $13$ to both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}5ky-13 & =7 \\ 5ky-13+13 & =7+13 \\ 5ky & =20\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide both sides of the equation by $5k\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}5ky & =20 \\ \frac{5ky}{5k} & =\frac{20}{5k} \\ \frac{\cancel{5k}y}{\cancel{5k}} & =\frac{20}{5k} \\ y & =\frac{20}{5k}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can further simplify the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\frac{5\cdot 4}{5k} \\ y & =\frac{\cancel{5}\cdot 4}{\cancel{5}k} \\ y & =\frac{4}{k}\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186179466 :question/problem "Solve the equation $\dfrac 34 kx + 9 = 2$ for the variable $x.$"] [17592186179466 :question/worked-solution "First, we multiply both sides of the equation by $4$ to get rid of the fraction:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{4}kx+9 & =2 \\ 4\cdot (\frac{3}{4}kx+9) & =4\cdot 2 \\ 3kx+36 & =8\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we need to isolate $x.$ To do this, we first subtract $36$ from both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}3kx+36 & =8 \\ 3kx+36-36 & =8-36 \\ 3kx & =-28\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide both sides of the equation by $3k\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}3kx & =-28 \\ \frac{3kx}{3k} & =\frac{-28}{3k} \\ \frac{\cancel{3k}x}{\cancel{3k}} & =\frac{-28}{3k} \\ x & =-\frac{28}{3k}\end{aligned}
$$"] [17592186179468 :question/problem "Solve the equation $\dfrac{1}{3} = -\dfrac{ax}{5}$ for the variable $x.$"] [17592186179468 :question/worked-solution "We need to isolate $x.$ To do this, we first cross-multiply:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} & =-\frac{ax}{5} \\ \frac{1}{3} & =\frac{-ax}{5} \\ 5\cdot 1 & =3\cdot (-ax) \\ 5 & =-3ax\end{aligned}

$$"] ["question-8bf4f7f2-b45d-5aef-8d47-16e8d1e1f900" :question/id #uuid "8bf4f7f2-b45d-5aef-8d47-16e8d1e1f900"] ["question-8bf4f7f2-b45d-5aef-8d47-16e8d1e1f900" :question/math-academy-id "q-214561"] ["question-8bf4f7f2-b45d-5aef-8d47-16e8d1e1f900" :question/problem "If $5=-14ab-2,$ then $a=${{field-1}}."] ["question-8bf4f7f2-b45d-5aef-8d47-16e8d1e1f900" :question/worked-solution "We need to isolate $a.$ To do this, we first add $2$ to both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =\frac{3}{10}hk \\ 10\cdot 2 & =10\cdot \frac{3}{10}hk \\ 20 & =3hk\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}-6xy & =10 \\ \frac{-6xy}{-6x} & =\frac{10}{-6x} \\ \frac{\cancel{-6x}\,y}{\cancel{-6x}} & =\frac{10}{-6x} \\ y & =-\frac{10}{6x}\end{aligned}
$$

We can further simplify the right-hand side as follows:
