define two more probability mass functions as follows:

- The **conditional probability mass function of $X$ given that $Y=y$,** denoted $f_{X|Y}(x|y),$ is defined as

$$
f_{X|Y}(x|y) = P(X = x \,|\, Y = y) = \dfrac{P(X = x, \, Y = y)}{P(Y=y)} = \dfrac{f(x,y)}{f_Y(y)},
$$

where  $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability mass function of $X$ and $Y,$ and $f_Y(y)$ is the marginal mass function of $Y.$

- The **conditional probability mass function of $Y$ given that $X=x,$** denoted $f_{Y|X}(y|x),$ is defined as

$$
f_{Y|X}(y|x) = P(Y = y \,|\, X = x) = \dfrac{P(X = x,\, Y = y)}{P(X=x)} = \dfrac{f(x,y)}{f_X(x)},
$$

where  $f(x,y)$ is a joint probability mass function of $X$ and $Y,$ and $f_X(x)$ is the marginal mass function of $X.$

**Watch out!** The conditional distribution of $X$ given $Y$ does *not* equal the conditional distribution of $Y$ given $X$. That is, in general,

$$
f_{X|Y}(x|y)  \ne f_{Y|X}(y|x).
$$

Finally, if $X$ and $Y$ are independent, then 

$$
f_{X|Y}(x|y)=f_X(x),\qquad f_{Y|X}(y|x)=f_Y(y).
$$

In other words, if $X$  and  $Y$ are independent, then knowing the value of one random variable does not affect the probability distribution of the other." :tutorial/id #uuid "1cbdc2c5-105c-5f9a-b4f4-7e4651bdc789" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6273 :tutorial/title "Conditional Probability Mass Functions"} :step/id #uuid "acc71c94-7794-57f0-bfff-16c3d8ed9e31" :step/math-academy-id 38019 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163066}}] :activity/title "Conditional Distributions for Discrete Random Variables" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186162164} {:db/id 17592186163004 :step/content {:db/id 17592186163288 :tutorial/content "Let's recall the multiplication law for conditional probability for two events ![](images/32/3207697e43e4f88223ad85c16964c3103a50c0c999a4ca14417695158d45526b.svg) and ![](images/5d/5d8b650b90c85fbc0db5e4b6fae61767e293a843d18a2526f3ee4157733e1f4b.svg)

two more probability mass functions as follows:

- The **conditional probability mass function of $X$ given that $Y=y$,** denoted $f_{X|Y}(x|y),$ is defined as

$$
f_{X|Y}(x|y) = P(X = x \,|\, Y = y) = \dfrac{P(X = x, \, Y = y)}{P(Y=y)} = \dfrac{f(x,y)}{f_Y(y)},
$$

where  $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability mass function of $X$ and $Y,$ and $f_Y(y)$ is the marginal mass function of $Y.$

- The **conditional probability mass function of $Y$ given that $X=x,$** denoted $f_{Y|X}(y|x),$ is defined as

$$
f_{Y|X}(y|x) = P(Y = y \,|\, X = x) = \dfrac{P(X = x,\, Y = y)}{P(X=x)} = \dfrac{f(x,y)}{f_X(x)},
$$

where  $f(x,y)$ is a joint probability mass function of $X$ and $Y,$ and $f_X(x)$ is the marginal mass function of $X.$

**Watch out!** The conditional distribution of $X$ given $Y$ does *not* equal the conditional distribution of $Y$ given $X$. That is, in general,

$$
f_{X|Y}(x|y)  \ne f_{Y|X}(y|x).
$$

Finally, if $X$ and $Y$ are independent, then 

$$
f_{X|Y}(x|y)=f_X(x),\qquad f_{Y|X}(y|x)=f_Y(y).
$$

In other words, if $X$  and  $Y$ are independent, then knowing the value of one random variable does not affect the probability distribution of the other." :tutorial/id #uuid "1cbdc2c5-105c-5f9a-b4f4-7e4651bdc789" :tutorial/math-academy-id 6273 :tutorial/title "Conditional Probability Mass Functions"} :step/id #uuid "acc71c94-7794-57f0-bfff-16c3d8ed9e31" :step/math-academy-id 38019 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163066}} {:db/id 17592186163065 :step/content {:db/id 17592186162104 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186161670 :question/id #uuid "2afabb9d-bd38-50f1-9afd-710ab839163c" :question/math-academy-id "e-10049"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ebabf742-2b8d-5392-a077-f34e8f4bd034" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186162317} {:db/id 17592186162374} {:db/id 17592186272384} {:db/id 17592186363335} {:db/id 17592186363342} {:db/id 17592186363349} {:db/id 17592186400965} {:db/id 17592186400972} {:db/id 17592186410511} {:db/id 17592186410513} {:db/id 17592186427208}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing a Conditional Probability Mass Function"} :step/id #uuid "000582c8-50ec-5bfc-b34a-c1cec0a03e2c" :step/math-academy-id 37921} {:db/id 17592186163066 :step/content {:db/id 17592186162105 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186161671 :question/id #uuid "0e42cf0f-f1bd-5762-a4fc-3cedec697c14" :question/math-academy-id "e-10050"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "277b8807-fb74-5ad3-a89b-92dbf90bc075" :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186162316} {:db/id 17592186162373} {:db/id 17592186363280} {:db/id 17592186363287} {:db/id 17592186363294} {:db/id 17592186363315} {:db/id 17592186410512} {:db/id 17592186410515}] :knowledge-point/title "Computing the Value of a Conditional Probability Mass Function at a Point"} :step/id #uuid "f16763f3-a2e5-5d38-9f53-ce65ea110dc5" :step/math-academy-id 37922 :step/next {:db/id 17592186163065}} {:db/id 17592186163325 :tutorial/content "We can now define two more probability mass functions as follows:

$$
{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=P(Y=y\,|\,X=x).
$$

Therefore, we're required to compute the conditional probability

$$
{f}_{Y|X}(3\,|\,3)=P(Y=3\,|\,X=3).
$$

By the multiplication law for conditional probability, we have

$$
P(Y=3\,|\,X=3)=\frac{P(X=3,Y=3)}{P(X=3)}=\frac{f(3,3)}{{f}_{X}(3)}
$$

where $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability mass function of $X$ and $Y,$ and ${f}_{X}(x)$ is the marginal distribution of $X.$

Recall that the marginal distribution for $X$ corresponds to the row totals. Thus, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(3) & =f(3,1)+f(3,2)+f(3,3) \\  & =\frac{5}{32}+\frac{5}{32}+\frac{3}{32} \\  & =\frac{13}{32}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given table, $f(3,3)=\frac{3}{32}.$ 

Finally, substituting  ${f}_{X}(3)=\frac{13}{32}$ and $f(3,3)=\frac{3}{32}$ in our formula above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y|X}(3\,|\,3) & =P(Y=3\,|\,X=3) \\  & =\frac{f(3,3)}{{f}_{X}(3)} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3}{32})}{(\frac{13}{32})} \\  & =\frac{3}{13}.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "21b7e9f5-9b6f-59bb-8de5-73acd87de7ec" :step/next {:db/id 17592186410517}} {:db/id 17592186410517 :step/content {:db/id 17592186410511 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "0c15b04c-20e5-50a7-9307-de1f9df589c6" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "| $y$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ |

Find the conditional probability mass function ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,3)$ given that the random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ shown in the table above." :question/worked-solution "The conditional probability mass function ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)$ is defined as

$$
{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,x)=P(Y=y\,|\,X=x).
$$

Therefore, we're required to compute the following set of conditional probabilities:

$$
{f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,3)=P(Y=y\,|\,X=3)
$$

By the multiplication law for conditional probability, we have

$$
P(Y=y\,|\,X=3)=\frac{P(X=3,Y=y)}{P(X=3)}=\frac{f(3,y)}{{f}_{X}(3)}
$$

where $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability mass function of $X$ and $Y,$ and ${f}_{X}(x)$ is the marginal distribution of $X.$

Recall that the marginal distributions for $X$ and $Y$ correspond to the row and column totals, respectively. So, let's compute these:

| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=3$ | ${f}_{X}(x)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=1$ | $0.15$ | $0.2$ | $0.05$ | $0.4$ |
| $X=3$ | $0.4$ | $0.1$ | $0.1$ | $0.6$ |
| ${f}_{Y}(y)$ | $0.55$ | $0.3$ | $0.15$ | $1$ |

Therefore, for $y\in {1,2,3},$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y=1\,|\,X=3) & =\frac{f(3,1)}{{f}_{X}(3)}=\frac{0.4}{0.6}=\frac{2}{3} \\ P(Y=2\,|\,X=3) & =\frac{f(3,2)}{{f}_{X}(3)}=\frac{0.1}{0.6}=\frac{1}{6} \\ P(Y=3\,|\,X=3) & =\frac{f(3,3)}{{f}_{X}(3)}=\frac{0.1}{0.6}=\frac{1}{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the conditional probability mass function can be represented by the following table:   

| $y$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${f}_{Y|X}(y\,|\,3)$ | $\frac{2}{3}$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ |"} :step/id #uuid "30942c86-dbc3-5faa-928f-8a3e27c6ef2a" :step/next {:db/id 17592186410520}} {:db/id 17592186410518 :step/content {:db/id 17592186410514 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1dea9c6c-8a37-5b15-a053-45fd4f8d2f9f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.6" :db/id 17592186410483} {:answer/id #uuid "c3b9f3ed-06e4-59ef-8471-d8398ce14731" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.25" :db/id 17592186410497} {:answer/id #uuid "d82990b6-7322-5310-a01d-936be990fc20" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.5" :db/id 17592186410501} {:answer/id #uuid "f4c7c149-9c87-52d8-aaf5-4888360f519e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.4" :db/id 17592186410504} {:answer/id #uuid "f7a8127b-532b-5c4e-95ea-e82e38e362d5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.75" :db/id 17592186410505}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410501} :answer-field/id #uuid "395c93a7-3493-526c-8001-2fe1cf196ffc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410507}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "b172bfa5-07a0-5df8-8d2d-99d558ae1db4" :question/math-academy-id "q-142896" :question/problem "| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=3$ | $Y=5$ |

Compute $P(0<X\le 6\,|\,Y=3)$ given that the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ shown in the table above." :question/worked-solution "By the multiplication law for conditional probability, the required conditional probability is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0<X\le 6\,|\,Y=3) & =\frac{P((0<X\le 6),Y=3)}{P(Y=3)} \\  & =\frac{P(X=3,Y=3)+P(X=6,Y=3)}{P(Y=3)} \\  & =\frac{f(3,3)+f(6,3)}{{f}_{Y}(3)},\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability mass function of $X$ and $Y,$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ is the marginal distribution of $Y.$

Recall that the marginal distribution for $Y$ corresponds to the column totals. Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(3) & =f(0,3)+f(3,3)+f(6,3)+f(9,3) \\  & =0+0.1+0+0.1 \\  & =0.2.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given table, we have that $f(3,3)=0.1$ and $f(6,3)=0.$ 

Finally, substituting our values into our formula above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0<X\le 6\,|\,Y=3) & =\frac{f(3,3)+f(6,3)}{{f}_{Y}(3)} \\  & =\frac{0.1+0}{0.2} \\  & =\frac{0.1}{0.2} \\  & =0.5.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "b0812b16-60e1-5ebb-80af-c271cd3f189c" :step/next {:db/id 17592186410516}} {:db/id 17592186410519 :step/content {:db/id 17592186410512 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "4176ad50-617b-5bbe-9749-530c4518c952" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.50" :db/id 17592186410486} {:answer/id #uuid "461964e4-b6e1-5a7d-85c6-1b999a2b0407" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.37" :db/id 17592186410487} {:answer/id #uuid "4deb08c4-9a80-57d4-8a91-17d29d971092" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.18" :db/id 17592186410488} {:answer/id #uuid "cb1bcdc1-72d1-5f68-bb9d-cd8c02cd1c36" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.42" :db/id 17592186410498} {:answer/id #uuid "d1106665-3f25-50f6-bf70-205dfb7d3993" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.13" :db/id 17592186410499}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410498} :answer-field/id #uuid "38673cd4-d233-5042-adf0-a6d70114ec93" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410506}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "70462da6-df40-572c-b721-518f7d0fb229" :question/math-academy-id "q-142893" :question/problem "| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ |

$$
{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,4)=P(X=x\,|\,Y=4)

By the multiplication law for conditional probability, we have

$$
P(X=x\,|\,Y=4)=\frac{P(X=x,Y=4)}{P(Y=4)}=\frac{f(x,4)}{{f}_{Y}(4)}
$$

where $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability mass function of $X$ and $Y,$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ is the marginal distribution of $Y.$

Recall that the marginal distributions for $X$ and $Y$ correspond to the row and column totals, respectively. So, let's compute these:

Find the conditional probability mass function ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,4)$ given that the random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ shown in the table above." :question/worked-solution "The conditional probability mass function ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)$ is defined as

$$
{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,y)=P(X=x\,|\,Y=y).
$$

Therefore, we're required to compute the following set of conditional probabilities:

$$
{f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,4)=P(X=x\,|\,Y=4)
$$

By the multiplication law for conditional probability, we have

$$
P(X=x\,|\,Y=4)=\frac{P(X=x,Y=4)}{P(Y=4)}=\frac{f(x,4)}{{f}_{Y}(4)}
$$

where $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability mass function of $X$ and $Y,$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ is the marginal distribution of $Y.$

Recall that the marginal distributions for $X$ and $Y$ correspond to the row and column totals, respectively. So, let's compute these:

| $f$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=2$ | $Y=4$ | ${f}_{X}(x)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=1$ | $0.15$ | $0.3$ | $0.1$ | $0.55$ |
| $X=2$ | $0$ | $0.2$ | $0.05$ | $0.25$ |
| $X=3$ | $0.05$ | $0.1$ | $0.05$ | $0.2$ |
| ${f}_{Y}(y)$ | $0.2$ | $0.6$ | $0.2$ | $1$ |

Therefore, for $x\in {1,2,3},$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=1\,|\,Y=4) & =\frac{f(1,4)}{{f}_{Y}(4)}=\frac{0.1}{0.2}=\frac{1}{2} \\ P(X=2\,|\,Y=4) & =\frac{f(2,4)}{{f}_{Y}(4)}=\frac{0.05}{0.2}=\frac{1}{4} \\ P(X=3\,|\,Y=4) & =\frac{f(3,4)}{{f}_{Y}(4)}=\frac{0.05}{0.2}=\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the conditional probability mass function can be represented by the following table:   

| $x$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${f}_{X|Y}(x\,|\,4)$ | $\frac{1}{2}$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ | $\frac{1}{4}$ |"} :step/id #uuid "e7c09165-5bb0-5525-a272-3f6aee4bdcee"} {:db/id 17592186410518 :step/content {:db/id 17592186410514 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1dea9c6c-8a37-5b15-a053-45fd4f8d2f9f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.6" :db/id 17592186410483} {:answer/id #uuid "c3b9f3ed-06e4-59ef-8471-d8398ce14731" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.25" :db/id 17592186410497} {:answer/id #uuid "d82990b6-7322-5310-a01d-936be990fc20" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.5" :db/id 17592186410501} {:answer/id #uuid "f4c7c149-9c87-52d8-aaf5-4888360f519e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.4" :db/id 17592186410504} {:answer/id #uuid "f7a8127b-532b-5c4e-95ea-e82e38e362d5" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "0.75" :db/id 17592186410505}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186410501} :answer-field/id #uuid "395c93a7-3493-526c-8001-2fe1cf196ffc" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186410507}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "b172bfa5-07a0-5df8-8d2d-99d558ae1db4" :question/math-academy-id "q-142896" :question/problem "| $f$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=3$ | $Y=5$ |

Compute $P(0<X\le 6\,|\,Y=3)$ given that the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ have the joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ shown in the table above." :question/worked-solution "By the multiplication law for conditional probability, the required conditional probability is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0<X\le 6\,|\,Y=3) & =\frac{P((0<X\le 6),Y=3)}{P(Y=3)} \\  & =\frac{P(X=3,Y=3)+P(X=6,Y=3)}{P(Y=3)} \\  & =\frac{f(3,3)+f(6,3)}{{f}_{Y}(3)},\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(x,y)$ is the joint probability mass function of $X$ and $Y,$ and ${f}_{Y}(y)$ is the marginal distribution of $Y.$

Recall that the marginal distribution for $Y$ corresponds to the column totals. Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(3) & =f(0,3)+f(3,3)+f(6,3)+f(9,3) \\  & =0+0.1+0+0.1 \\  & =0.2.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given table, we have that $f(3,3)=0.1$ and $f(6,3)=0.$ 

Finally, substituting our values into our formula above, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}P(0<X\le 6\,|\,Y=3) & =\frac{f(3,3)+f(6,3)}{{f}_{Y}(3)} \\  & =\frac{0.1+0}{0.2} \\  & =\frac{0.1}{0.2} \\  & =0.5.\end{aligned}
$$"} :step/id #uuid "b0812b16-60e1-5ebb-80af-c271cd3f189c" :step/next {:db/id 17592186410516}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "1dea9c6c-8a37-5b15-a053-45fd4f8d2f9f" :answer/type {:db/id For example, consider the matrix

![](images/6c/6c03ab3dfd7b75c9a89defe102f33946da200fb88d26139e54c889a90467068a.svg)
where we denote its columns by $\color{red}\mathbf{a}_1$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2},$ respectively. The column space of this matrix is given by
![](images/5f/5faad23bc77f821d42223beaca06364e38c7f0ba8a4869cb138e0e923e90b8f7.svg)

Now, suppose we would like to determine whether the vector ![](images/45/45349edee356334c54ad85a6d60757a6a7833a392962086815a2436446e323dc.svg) lies in $\textrm{Col}(A).$ In other words, we need to check if $\mathbf{b} \in \textrm{Span}\{ {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}.$ So, we need to determine whether $\mathbf{b}$ can be written as some linear combination of $\color{red}\mathbf{a}_1$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}=b\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the equation above can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & {a}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =b \\ {{[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{x}} & ={{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{b}}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equation is equivalent to $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}.$ To solve the equation, let's find the row echelon form of the augmented matrix $[A \,|\, \mathbf{b}]$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[A\,|\,b] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 & -3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & -7 & -7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=2 \\ -7{x}_{2}=-7.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get $x_2=1.$ Substituting into the first equation, we get $x_1=-1.$

Since we have a solution, the equation $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ is consistent, which implies that $\mathbf{b} \in \textrm{Col}(A).$

Moreover, there is exactly one solution, so we have exactly one way to write $\mathbf{b}$ as a linear combination of $\color{red}\mathbf{a}_1$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}\mathbin{:}$
![](images/a3/a3965a53b3b3cfda2e11c4a68ba882631dc2763f32de67de30b4751aca76f2e5.svg)" :tutorial/id #uuid "f65da145-207a-50c6-b59e-8756d247cc71" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3201 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "e2b22098-86e0-53ea-bbc9-fc31b60b4152" :step/math-academy-id 17489 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120681}} {:db/id 17592186120681 :step/content {:db/id 17592186119810 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id 17592186119621 :question/id #uuid "244793f6-41c3-5920-9264-bec32cda9c9c" :question/math-academy-id "e-4807"} :knowledge-point/id #uuid "5c8e217c-252d-529f-a810-84787e2ee886" :knowledge-point/key-prerequisites [{:db/id 17592186048315}] :knowledge-point/questions [{:db/id 17592186120313} {:db/id 17592186120339} {:db/id 17592186247182} {:db/id 17592186247183} {:db/id 17592186247185} {:db/id 17592186317417} {:db/id 17592186342180} {:db/id 17592186408163} {:db/id 17592186430002}] :knowledge-point/title "Determining if a Vector is in the Column Space of a Matrix"} :step/id #uuid "415a39b4-7da9-55ac-afde-f8932b3c0813" :step/math-academy-id 17491 :step/next {:db/id 17592186120749}} {:db/id 17592186120682 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121038 :tutorial/content "The column space is defined for matrices of *any* dimensions. In general, if ${\color{black}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{black}\mathbf{a}_2}, \ldots, {\color{black}\mathbf{a}_n}$ are the columns of a matrix $A,$ that is to say,
![](images/d9/d9d3fd7384b4375895d234c22c9d81f30358439f7e04ee8db055de9d5d7f1174.svg)
then $\textrm{Col}(A) = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{black}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{black}\mathbf{a}_2}, \ldots, {\color{black}\mathbf{a}_n} \}.$

The column space satisfies the following properties:

- If $A$ is an ${\color{blue}m}\times n$ matrix, then $\textrm{Col}(A)$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^{\color{blue}m}.$ This is because each column has ${\color{blue}m}$ entries.

(i.e., the set of all possible linear combinations of columns of $A$). For example, consider the matrix

![](images/6c/6c03ab3dfd7b75c9a89defe102f33946da200fb88d26139e54c889a90467068a.svg)
where we denote its columns by $\color{red}\mathbf{a}_1$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2},$ respectively. The column space of this matrix is given by
![](images/5f/5faad23bc77f821d42223beaca06364e38c7f0ba8a4869cb138e0e923e90b8f7.svg)

Now, suppose we would like to determine whether the vector ![](images/45/45349edee356334c54ad85a6d60757a6a7833a392962086815a2436446e323dc.svg) lies in $\textrm{Col}(A).$ In other words, we need to check if $\mathbf{b} \in \textrm{Span}\{ {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}.$ So, we need to determine whether $\mathbf{b}$ can be written as some linear combination of $\color{red}\mathbf{a}_1$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}=b\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that the equation above can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{a}_{1} & {a}_{2}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =b \\ {{[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{A}{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{x}} & ={{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{b}}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the equation is equivalent to $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}.$ To solve the equation, let's find the row echelon form of the augmented matrix $[A \,|\, \mathbf{b}]$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[A\,|\,b] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 & -3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 2 \\ 0 & -7 & -7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=2 \\ -7{x}_{2}=-7.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get $x_2=1.$ Substituting into the first equation, we get $x_1=-1.$

Since we have a solution, the equation $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ is consistent, which implies that $\mathbf{b} \in \textrm{Col}(A).$

Moreover, there is exactly one solution, so we have exactly one way to write $\mathbf{b}$ as a linear combination of $\color{red}\mathbf{a}_1$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}\mathbin{:}$

Determine if $b\in \text{Col}(A).$ 
In the affirmative case, find the value of ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}\cdot {x}_{3}$, where ${x}_{1},{x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ are real numbers such that $b={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}{a}_{3},$ and ${a}_{1}$, ${a}_{2}$, and ${a}_{3}$ are the respective columns of $A.$

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -8 \\ 0 & -1 & 4 \\ 2 & 0 & -4\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]
$$" :question/worked-solution "In order to determine whether $b$ lies in $\text{Col}(A),$ we need to check if the equation $Ax=b$ is consistent. So, let's find the row echelon form of the augmented matrix $[A\,|\,b]$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[A\,|\,b] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -8 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 & -4 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -8 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 4 & 2 \\ 0 & -6 & 12 & 6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-6){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -8 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 4 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & -12 & -6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we have the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}-8{x}_{3}=-2 \\ -{x}_{2}+4{x}_{3}=2 \\ -12{x}_{3}=-6.\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get ${x}_{3}=\frac{1}{2}.$ Substituting it into the second equation gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2}+4(\frac{1}{2}) & =2 \\ -{x}_{2}+2 & =2 \\ {x}_{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, from the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+3(0)-8(\frac{1}{2}) & =-2 \\ {x}_{1}-4 & =-2 \\ {x}_{1} & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we have a solution, the equation $Ax=b$ is consistent, which implies that $b\in \text{Col}(A).$ 

Moreover, there is exactly one solution, so we have exactly one way to write $b$ as a linear combination of ${a}_{1},$ ${a}_{2},$ and ${a}_{3}:$

$$
{{[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{b}=2\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{1}}+0\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{2}}+\frac{1}{2}\cdot {{[\begin{aligned}-8 \\ 4 \\ -4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{{a}_{3}}
$$

Finally, we get ${x}_{1}\cdot {x}_{2}\cdot {x}_{3}=2\cdot 0\cdot \frac{1}{2}=0.$"} :step/id #uuid "a4bd27de-27e6-5be6-9522-5db3c45dc351" :step/next {:db/id 17592186424111}} {:answer-field/choices :question/math-academy-id "q-110978" :question/problem "Consider the matrix given by $A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}].$ Determine the value of $k$ for which the vector $b=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 12 \\ k+30\end{aligned}]$ belongs to $\text{Col}(A).$" :question/worked-solution "If $b$ lies in $\text{Col}(A),$ then the equation $Ax=b$ must be consistent. So, let's find the row echelon form of the augmented matrix $[A\,|\,b]$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[A\,|\,b] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & -3 \\ 1 & 1 & 12 \\ 0 & 5 & k+30\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & ↔{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 12 \\ -2 & 1 & -3 \\ 0 & 5 & k+30\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 12 \\ 0 & 3 & 21 \\ 0 & 5 & k+30\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=(\frac{1}{3}){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 12 \\ 0 & 1 & 7 \\ 0 & 5 & k+30\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-5{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 12 \\ 0 & 1 & 7 \\ 0 & 0 & k-5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the system

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=12 \\ {x}_{2}=7 \\ 0=k-5.\end{aligned}
$$

In order for this system to be consistent, we require $0=k-5,$ which means that $k=5.$"} :step/id #uuid "8889818c-a946-5d8d-bda5-8076c4a7ea11" :step/next {:db/id 17592186481449}} - A normal vector to the plane ${\Pi_{{1}}}$  is $\mathbf{n}_1 = \langle 2,\:-1,\: 1 \rangle.$

- A normal vector to the plane ${\Pi_{{2}}}$  is $\mathbf{n}_2 = \langle -1,\: 1,\: -1 \rangle.$

If two distinct planes intersect each other, their intersection will always be a straight line. A direction vector $\mathbf{v}$ for that line can be found by computing the cross product of the normal vectors of the two planes. 

![](images/0c/0cf233086eccae47e640d3599908572e2c3a9996dd84d861e4d659c03108105c.png)

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}v & ={n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} \\  & =⟨2,\,-1,\,1⟩\times ⟨-1,\,1,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =j+k \\  & =⟨0,1,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$" :tutorial/id #uuid "1e276ddb-1c14-51fd-8261-8c02eb3294f0" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3803 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "1ae4dc56-971c-585e-ac6e-a1d1927975cc" :step/math-academy-id :step/next {:db/id 17592186148281}} {:db/id 17592186148280 :step/content {:db/id 17592186148744 :tutorial/content "In general, given two planes 

$$
{\Pi_{{1}}}\mathbin{:} \quad a_{1}x+b_{1}y + c_{1}z+ d_1=0 \qquad  \text{and} \qquad   {\Pi_{{2}}}\mathbin{:} \quad a_{2}x+b_{2}y + c_{2}z+ d_2=0,
$$

 we have the following cases, regarding the positions of their normal vectors  $\mathbf{n}_1$ and $\mathbf{n}_2 \mathbin{:}$ 

- *Case 1*:  If $\mathbf{n}_1\nparallel \mathbf{n}_2$ then ${\Pi_{{1}}}$   and ${\Pi_{{2}}}$ intersect on a straight line.

- *Case 2*:  If $\mathbf{n}_1\parallel \mathbf{n}_2$ but the corresponding equations of the planes are not scalar multiples of each other, then the planes are distinct and are parallel to each other.

- *Case 3*:  If the corresponding coefficients of ${\Pi_{{1}}}$ and ${\Pi_{{2}}}$ are all proportional, then the planes are coincident." :tutorial/id #uuid "50ffbdb5-c9d0-5815-9b29-b505cde7f0fa" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3804 :tutorial/title "Intersection of Two Planes in 3D"} :step/id #uuid "cba5c95d-7e83-5872-ae95-b6832ff486a2" :step/math-academy-id 21955 :step/next {:db/id 17592186148279}} {:db/id 17592186148281 :step/content {:db/id 17592186148745 :tutorial/content "Consider a line that is given by its vector equation
![](images/ca/ca43fd13bd65c544d66a4de2801871c2a79087fd960db44696ce6068d30c8377.svg)

Since $y=2$ at every point on the line, the corresponding Cartesian equations of this line are

$$
\dfrac{x-1}2 =z+1, \quad y=2.
$$

We may therefore interpret this line as the intersection of the planes $\dfrac{x-1}2 =z+1$ and $y=2$.

Let's look at one more example. Given the line 

![](images/1a/1a97b5bcff75bc7306d14a8af3fb1f169a2e7bf865be2e7a9c6d2741eecc63a6.svg)

we can write its Cartesian equation as

$$
\dfrac{x-2}{-5}=\dfrac{y-1}2 = \dfrac{z-1}3
$$

which can be further written as the system of two equations:

![](images/1f/1f4cce850809f3fda876dd96e1cf9c65fd873df97bbba44e291b611896c86ca4.svg)

So, again, our line can be represented as the intersection of the planes $2x+5y-9=0$ and $3y-2z-1=0$." :tutorial/id #uuid "a7303bab-ef2c-5a9b-9caa-dc6fcc7929d2" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3817 :tutorial/title "The Cartesian Equation of a Line as the Intersection of Two Planes"} :step/id #uuid "8aec20bb-3034-54e2-b58d-43a8fc04ec0d" :step/math-academy-id 22145}] :activity/title "The Intersection of Two Planes" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186147718} {:db/id 17592186148276 :step/content {:db/id 17592186148743 :tutorial/content "Suppose we are given the planes ${\Pi_{{1}}}: 2x -y+z=0$ and ${\Pi_{{2}}}: -x + y-z=1.$ First, notice that:

"q-71465" :question/problem "Given the two planes $x+y+z=0$ and $x+y+1=0$, which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** The cross product of the normal vectors of the planes is equal to $⟨1,1,0⟩.$

- **II.** The planes intersect on a line.

- **III.** The planes are coincident." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that:

- For the plane $x+y+z=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,1,1⟩.$

- For the plane $x+y+1=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,1,0⟩.$

Now, let's consider the statements.

- Statement I is false. Indeed, computing the cross product of the normal vectors, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,1,1⟩\times ⟨1,1,0⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i+j \\  & =⟨-1,1,0⟩\ne ⟨1,1,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Since ${n}_{1}\times {n}_{2}\ne 0$, the vectors ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are not parallel. Hence, the corresponding planes must intersect on a line.

- Statement III is false. Indeed, two non-parallel planes could not be coincident either.

Therefore, only statement II is true."} :step/id #uuid "0311a340-7168-5cea-821e-a5c70f05f78d" :step/next {:db/id 17592186421907}} {:db/id 17592186421904 :step/content {:db/id 17592186262998 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "2bbb0f75-5837-5fef-9156-1bb0626a6799" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{a}_{1}+{a}_{2}=-3,\,b=⟨-1,1,2⟩" :db/id 17592186260264} {:answer/id #uuid "358aeb92-2af7-5b63-a3fc-98a16739711a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{a}_{1}+{a}_{2}=6,\,b=⟨-2,1,1⟩" :db/id 17592186260355} {:answer/id #uuid "4ae1bb4f-6418-5cbe-8748-f187b44dbec8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{a}_{1}+{a}_{2}=3,\,b=⟨-1,2,1⟩" :db/id 17592186260517} {:answer/id #uuid "83b18a92-b695-5c83-b721-b2dee329f376" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{a}_{1}+{a}_{2}=-6,\,b=⟨-2,1,-1⟩" :db/id 17592186261019} {:answer/id #uuid "db99d772-027a-5c17-b647-51f20577ed39" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "{a}_{1}+{a}_{2}=5,\,b=⟨1,2,1⟩" :db/id 17592186261817}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186260517} :answer-field/id #uuid "3e5261fb-a30e-5c21-b272-d448a6432184" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186262235}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "ad00dc96-c374-5320-be1d-ca73d7e96f79" :question/math-academy-id "q-129238" :question/problem "The intersection of the planes $x+y-z-3=0$ and $x+2y-3z+18=0$ is given by the line

$$
r(t)=⟨{a}_{1},{a}_{2},0⟩+tb,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).
$$

Calculate ${a}_{1}+{a}_{2},$ and find a possible direction vector $b.$" :question/worked-solution "We're given that there exists a point on the line where $z=0.$ Substituting this into the first equation gives  

$$
x+y-0-3=0\,⟹\,x=3-y,
$$

and substituting $z=0$ and $x=3-y$ into the second equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(3-y)+2y-3(0)+18 & =0 \\ 3+y+18 & =0 \\ y & =-21.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $x=3-y=3+21=24$ and $a=⟨24,-21,0⟩$ is a position vector of a point on the line.

Next, we notice:

- For the plane $x+y-z-3=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,1,-1⟩.$

- For the plane $x+2y-3z+18=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,2,-3⟩.$

To find a direction vector for the line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,1,-1⟩\times ⟨1,2,-3⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & -3\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i+2j+k \\  & =⟨-1,2,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the equation of the line is:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+tb \\ r(t) & =⟨24,-21,0⟩+t⟨-1,2,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally then, ${a}_{1}+{a}_{2}=24-21=3,$ and $b=⟨-1,2,1⟩.$"} :step/id #uuid "4b62f78b-d432-5341-a2aa-4388a4c716e4"} {:db/id 17592186421905 :step/content {:db/id 17592186338949 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3e2afd41-011d-50b7-bdd6-b2fe0e79319a" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186451519} {:answer/id #uuid "f1a8a6a1-4d09-5b9a-87bf-b8affe56cc46" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186451520}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186451519} :answer-field/id #uuid "c4ff5205-ba68-5bf5-9b0a-caec3fa1d55c" :answer-field/key "I" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186452607} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "c4573706-4ddd-5c59-ae75-f76209f442b7" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186451521} {:answer/id #uuid "8a64a65e-cbd5-5aa2-9fc1-b39766e3b1ef" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186451522}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186451521} :answer-field/id #uuid "a02ea405-f5ad-5f66-b8b5-c7c965e15944" :answer-field/key "II" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186452608} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "86e1367f-c77e-5db8-87a9-df2724a72ab1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "false" :db/id 17592186451523} {:answer/id #uuid "bdf169b7-e727-58e0-a834-1eca473c044e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045499} :answer/value "true" :db/id 17592186451524}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186451524} :answer-field/id #uuid "7ecb6f3e-52a7-56a2-9a87-95a8d2a508e8" :answer-field/key "III" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186408166} :db/id 17592186452609}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/id #uuid "894f2787-9676-52de-a718-3b82f8fd7a1d" :question/math-academy-id "q-71463" :question/problem "Given the two planes $3x+3y+2z=0$ and $x-y-z=0$, which of the following statements are true?

Calculate ${a}_{2}-{a}_{3},$ and find a possible direction vector $b.$" :question/worked-solution "We're given that there exists a point on the line where $x=0.$ Substituting this to the first equation gives

$$
0+3y-3=0\,⟹\,y=1,
$$

and substituting $x=0$ into the second equation gives

$$
0+z+19=0\,⟹\,z=-19.
$$

Therefore, $a=⟨0,1,-19⟩$ is a position vector of a point on the line.

Next, we notice:

- For the plane $2x+3y-3=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨2,3,0⟩.$

- For the plane $3x+z+19=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨3,0,1⟩.$

To find a direction vector for the line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}b & ={n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} \\  & =⟨2,3,0⟩\times ⟨3,0,1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 3 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =3i-2j-9k \\  & =⟨3,-2,-9⟩\end{aligned}
$$

The equation of the line is:

$$

- **I.** The cross product of the normal vectors of the planes is equal to $⟨1,6,-5⟩.$

- **II.** The planes are parallel.

- **III.** The planes intersect on a line." :question/worked-solution "First, notice that:

- For the plane $3x+3y+2z=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨3,3,2⟩.$

- For the plane $x-y-z=0,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,-1,-1⟩.$

Now, let's consider the statements.

- Statement I is false. Computing the cross product of the normal vectors, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨3,3,2⟩\times ⟨1,-1,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 3 & 3 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i+5j-6k \\  & =⟨-1,5,-6⟩\ne ⟨1,6,-5⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Since ${n}_{1}\times {n}_{2}\ne 0$, the vectors ${n}_{1}$ and ${n}_{2}$ are not parallel. As a result, the corresponding planes are not parallel either.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, two non-parallel planes in $3$-dimensional space must intersect on a line.

Therefore, only statement III is true."} :step/id #uuid "8993a320-0fa1-5bea-8343-47ddcfb4405b" :step/next {:db/id 17592186421903}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "$$
V=\text{Span}\{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]\},\,B=\{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]\}
$$

Consider the subspace $V$ and an orthogonal basis $B$ of $V,$ given above. Given that $B$ is derived from $V$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, what is the value of $\frac{b}{a}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's denote 

$\,$ ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{aligned}].$ 

We proceed to find an orthogonal basis using the Gram-Schmidt process, as follows.

**Step 1**: We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 2**: Next, we find ${v}_{2}$, by using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for ${v}_{2}$ in our case gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{4\cdot 3+2\cdot 0+(-3)\cdot (-1)}{{3}^{2}+{0}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]-\frac{3}{2}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 2 \\ -\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $B=\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\}=\{[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 2 \\ -\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}]\}$ is an orthogonal basis for $V.$

Finally, we have $a=-\frac{1}{2},$ $b=2,$ and 

$$
\frac{b}{a}=\frac{2}{(-\frac{1}{2})}=-4.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186414753 :question/id #uuid "c7bb7823-c38b-5250-a2f7-3b306162dae1" :question/math-academy-id "q-40736" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "048ef5c8-0a10-53a5-bbcf-1d721a524144" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7}{13}" :db/id 17592186414721} {:answer/id #uuid "05da9795-05f5-5040-9da5-00cee056fe08" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{13}{15}" :db/id 17592186414722} {:answer/id #uuid "1326ecd9-681d-55f9-841c-c7013851f621" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{17}{11}" :db/id 17592186414723} {:answer/id #uuid "292aa1fd-4f1b-5b3f-b502-e340aa086aa9" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{12}{7}" :db/id 17592186414726} {:answer/id #uuid "502fbad5-6108-585e-9a6e-c3c7e917352d" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{15}{13}" :db/id 17592186414727}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186414723} :answer-field/id #uuid "219cb7dd-0360-5f51-af53-0c31b7c77c47" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186414745}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045487} :question/problem "$$

$$

Consider the subspace $V$ and an orthogonal basis $B$ of $V,$ given above. Given that $B$ is derived from $V$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, what is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's denote 

$\,$ ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ 

We proceed to find an orthogonal basis using the Gram-Schmidt process, as follows.

**Step 1**: We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{aligned}].$

**Step 2**: Next, we find ${v}_{2}$, by using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for ${v}_{2}$ in our case gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{3\cdot 1+2\cdot 1+2\cdot (-2)}{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+(-2)^{2}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{17}{6} \\ \frac{11}{6} \\ \frac{7}{3}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $B={{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}\frac{17}{6} \\ \frac{11}{6} \\ \frac{7}{3}\end{aligned}]}$ is an orthogonal basis for $V.$

Finally, we have $a=\frac{17}{6},$ $b=\frac{11}{6},$ and 

$$
\frac{a}{b}=\frac{(\frac{17}{6})}{(\frac{11}{6})}=\frac{17}{11}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186481350 :question/id #uuid "17e0153f-17ba-57ee-a920-3117ebdc5b12" :question/math-academy-id "q-140524"} {:db/id 17592186481360 :question/id #uuid A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,B={[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]}
$$

Consider the subspace $\text{Col}(A)$ and an orthogonal basis $B$ of $\text{Col}(A),$ where $A$ and $B$ are given above. Given that $B$ is derived from $\text{Col}(A)$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, what is the value of $\frac{b}{a}?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that $\text{Col}(A)$ is the span of the columns of $A.$ 

First, let's denote

$\,$ ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ 

We proceed to find an orthogonal basis using the Gram-Schmidt process, as follows.

**Step 1**: We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

**Step 2**: Next, we find ${v}_{2}$, by using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for ${v}_{2}$ in our case gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{2\cdot 3+1\cdot (-1)+2\cdot 0}{{3}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{0}^{2}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]-\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{3}{2} \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $B={{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}={[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{3}{2} \\ 2\end{aligned}]}$ is an orthogonal basis for $\text{Col}(A).$

Finally, $a=\frac{1}{2},$ $b=\frac{3}{2},$ and  

$$
\frac{b}{a}=\frac{(\frac{3}{2})}{(\frac{1}{2})}=3.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186134337 :question/id #uuid "4388fdfa-5eb8-5165-a253-2f6080a33d4c" :question/math-academy-id "q-41035"} {:db/id 17592186272123 :question/id #uuid 17592186045485 :db/ident :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & 5 \\ 1 & 6\end{aligned}],\,B={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]}
$$

Consider the subspace $\text{Col}(A)$ and an orthogonal basis $B$ of $\text{Col}(A),$ where $A$ and $B$ are given above. Given that $B$ is derived from $\text{Col}(A)$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, what is the value of $\frac{b}{c}?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that $\text{Col}(A)$ is the span of the columns of $A.$  

First, let's denote

$\,$ ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5 \\ 6\end{aligned}].$ 

We proceed to find an orthogonal basis using the Gram-Schmidt process, as follows.

**Step 1**: We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 2**: Next, we find ${v}_{2}$, by using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for ${v}_{2}$ in our case gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{2\cdot 1+5\cdot (-1)+6\cdot 1}{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 5 \\ 6\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 6 \\ 5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $B={{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 6 \\ 5\end{aligned}]}$ is an orthogonal basis for $\text{Col}(A).$

Finally, $b=6,$ $c=5,$ and  

$$
\frac{b}{c}=\frac{6}{5}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186354525 :question/id #uuid "32ca7514-6be2-5643-9bb9-256990a44ecc" :question/math-academy-id "q-86850"} {:db/id 17592186366125 :question/id #uuid {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/problem "$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ -2 & 0 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}],\,B={{u}_{1},{u}_{2}}={[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]}
$$

Consider the subspace $\text{Col}(A)$ and an **orthonormal** basis $B$ of $\text{Col}(A),$ where $A$ and $B$ are given above. Given that $B$ is derived from $\text{Col}(A)$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, what is the value of $|a|+|b|+|c|?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that $\text{Col}(A)$ is the span of the columns of $A.$  

First, let's denote

$\,$ ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ -3\end{aligned}].$ 

We proceed to find an orthogonal basis using the Gram-Schmidt process, as follows.

**Step 1**: We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

**Step 2**: Next, we find ${v}_{2}$, by using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for ${v}_{2}$ in our case gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{3\cdot (-1)+0\cdot (-2)+(-3)\cdot 2}{{1}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ -3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we normalize each vector to get an orthonormal basis:

- ${u}_{1}=\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}].$

- ${u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3} \\ -\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}].$

Therefore, $B={{u}_{1},{u}_{2}}={[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3} \\ -\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]}$ is an orthonormal basis for $\text{Col}(A).$

Finally, $a=\frac{2}{3},$ $b=-\frac{2}{3},$ $c=-\frac{1}{3}$ and  

$$
|a|+|b|+|c|=|\frac{2}{3}|+|-\frac{2}{3}|+|-\frac{1}{3}|=\frac{5}{3}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186272129 :question/id #uuid "3a029be5-b6a5-506a-8947-8d15614953ac" :question/math-academy-id "q-140537" :knowledge-point/_questions [{:db/id 17592186133795 :knowledge-point/id #uuid "ccdefb8e-1bb5-52e9-812d-d2a5bffff731" :knowledge-point/title "Finding an Orthonormal Basis of a Vector Space"}] :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "268ee3f5-ff62-526c-bf07-b0aae6059055" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{2\sqrt{6}}{3}" :db/id 17592186269608} {:answer/id #uuid "a4e320c7-d04c-5cac-8eca-b6a622015283" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{6}}{6}" :db/id 17592186270744} {:answer/id #uuid "a762e70a-2bf7-5828-83b6-2879ecead2de" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{\sqrt{6}}{3}" :db/id 17592186270767} {:answer/id #uuid "e23a2964-03f4-55d3-83a8-a9094a21cbd8" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\sqrt{6}" :db/id 17592186271257} {:answer/id #uuid "e42fb063-1a4d-51c6-9072-fbbe5660f809" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "2\sqrt{6}" :db/id 17592186271281}] :answer-field/correct {:answer/id #uuid "268ee3f5-ff62-526c-bf07-b0aae6059055" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498 :db/ident :answer.type/math} :answer/value "\frac{2\sqrt{6}}{3}" :db/id 17592186269608} :answer-field/id #uuid "2972b933-504c-5f0a-b4df-b81a8c22a6e7" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493 :db/ident :answer-field.type/radio} :db/id 17592186271587}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "$$

$$

Consider the subspace $V$ and an **orthonormal** basis $B$ of $V,$ given above. Given that $B$ is derived from $V$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, what is the value of $|a|+|b|+|c|?$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's denote

$\,$ ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ 

We proceed to find an orthogonal basis using the Gram-Schmidt process, as follows.

**Step 1**: We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

**Step 2**: Next, we find ${v}_{2}$, by using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for ${v}_{2}$ in our case gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{2\cdot 1+2\cdot 0+0\cdot 1}{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we normalize each vector to get an orthonormal basis:

- ${u}_{1}=\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ 0 \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}].$

- ${u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{(-1)}^{2}}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{6}}{6} \\ \frac{\sqrt{6}}{3} \\ -\frac{\sqrt{6}}{6}\end{aligned}].$

Therefore, $B={{u}_{1},{u}_{2}}={[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ 0 \\ \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{6}}{6} \\ \frac{\sqrt{6}}{3} \\ -\frac{\sqrt{6}}{6}\end{aligned}]}$ is an  orthonormal basis of $V.$   

Finally, $a=\frac{\sqrt{6}}{6},$ $b=\frac{\sqrt{6}}{3},$ $c=-\frac{\sqrt{6}}{6}$ and   

$$

17592186414749}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486 :db/ident :question.difficulty/hard} :question/problem "$$
V=\text{Span}{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4 \\ 2\end{aligned}]},\,B={[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{14}}{7} \\ \frac{\sqrt{14}}{14} \\ \frac{3\sqrt{14}}{14}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]}
$$

Consider the subspace $V$ and an **orthonormal** basis $B$ of $V,$ given above. Given that $B$ is derived from $V$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, what is the value of $|a|+|b|+|c|?$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's denote

$\,$ ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ 

We proceed to find an orthogonal basis using the Gram-Schmidt process, as follows.

**Step 1**: We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$

**Step 2**: Next, we find ${v}_{2}$, by using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for ${v}_{2}$ in our case gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{2\cdot 2+4\cdot 1+2\cdot 3}{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4 \\ 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we normalize each vector to get an orthonormal basis.

- ${u}_{1}=\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{14}}{7} \\ \frac{\sqrt{14}}{14} \\ \frac{3\sqrt{14}}{14}\end{aligned}].$

- ${u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{3}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ \frac{3\sqrt{10}}{10} \\ -\frac{\sqrt{10}}{10}\end{aligned}].$

Therefore, $B={{u}_{1},{u}_{2}}={[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{14}}{7} \\ \frac{\sqrt{14}}{14} \\ \frac{3\sqrt{14}}{14}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ \frac{3\sqrt{10}}{10} \\ -\frac{\sqrt{10}}{10}\end{aligned}]}$ is an orthonormal basis for $V.$

Finally, $a=0,$ $b=\frac{3\sqrt{10}}{10},$ $c=-\frac{\sqrt{10}}{10}$ and  

$$
|a|+|b|+|c|=|\,0\,|+|\frac{3\sqrt{10}}{10}|+|-\frac{\sqrt{10}}{10}|=\frac{2\sqrt{10}}{5}.
$$"} {:db/id 17592186481433 :question/id #uuid "ed119e3d-d405-5ea0-ae9c-40defc91b776" :question/math-academy-id "q-86852"} {:db/id 17592186049864} {:db/id 17592186050539} {:answer-field/choices 2127} :activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186134684 :step/content {:db/id 17592186135054 :tutorial/content "The **Gram-Schmidt process** is an algorithm that we can use to construct an *orthogonal* basis if we are given a non-orthogonal basis to start with.

For example, consider the basis $\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}$ for the subspace $V=\textrm{Span} \{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \},$ where
![](images/c2/c2543117bc661286a5965534dfeeaaf6a066281ee58e2f39ea35143971d6837f.svg)

We can use the above basis to construct an *orthogonal* basis for the given $2$-dimensional subspace. To do this, we use the Gram-Schmidt process, which involves $2$ steps:

- **Step 1:** Set ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1}=\mathbf{a}_1.$

- **Step 2:** Find a vector $\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2$ in $V$ that's orthogonal to $\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1.$ This can be achieved by computing

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}\,-\,{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}\,{a}_{2} \\  & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/67/678cc056e3c9d3fbf17423ac591b3e85d84ee8060c0637840fe1c4c9e87aa878.png)

Notice that $\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2$ is written as a linear combination of $\mathbf{a}_1(={\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1})$ and $\mathbf{a}_2.$ So this means that ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2} \in V,$ and also ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2} \perp {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1}.$
Moreover, 

$$
\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2\} = V = \textrm{Span}\{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2} \}.
$$

After applying the Gram-Schmidt process, we get the set $\mathcal{B}=\{{\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2}\},$ which is an orthogonal basis for $V.$

So, in our example, we start by setting ![](images/72/7221215504f7dc7a831501ee23c0563434dd414ac05c1ef7e5761c2719e7d24d.svg) Then, we find the vector $\mathbf{v}_2$ that's orthogonal to $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{v}_1\}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1} \\  & ={a}_{2}-\frac{4\cdot 1+6\cdot (-1)}{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6\end{aligned}]-(-1)\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

For example, consider the basis $\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}$ for the subspace $V=\textrm{Span} \{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \},$ where
![](images/c2/c2543117bc661286a5965534dfeeaaf6a066281ee58e2f39ea35143971d6837f.svg)

We can use the above basis to construct an *orthogonal* basis for the given $2$-dimensional subspace. To do this, we use the Gram-Schmidt process, which involves $2$ steps:

- **Step 1:** Set ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1}=\mathbf{a}_1.$

- **Step 2:** Find a vector $\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2$ in $V$ that's orthogonal to $\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1.$ This can be achieved by computing

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}\,-\,{\text{proj}}_{{v}_{1}}\,{a}_{2} \\  & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/67/678cc056e3c9d3fbf17423ac591b3e85d84ee8060c0637840fe1c4c9e87aa878.png)

Notice that $\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2$ is written as a linear combination of $\mathbf{a}_1(={\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1})$ and $\mathbf{a}_2.$ So this means that ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2} \in V,$ and also ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2} \perp {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1}.$
Moreover, 

$$
\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2\} = V = \textrm{Span}\{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2} \}.
$$

After applying the Gram-Schmidt process, we get the set $\mathcal{B}=\{{\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2}\},$ which is an orthogonal basis for $V.$

So, in our example, we start by setting ![](images/72/7221215504f7dc7a831501ee23c0563434dd414ac05c1ef7e5761c2719e7d24d.svg) Then, we find the vector $\mathbf{v}_2$ that's orthogonal to $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{v}_1\}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1} \\  & ={a}_{2}-\frac{4\cdot 1+6\cdot (-1)}{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 6\end{aligned}]-(-1)\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ![](images/59/5944c42ffd5e609dcec914718180be9652a817de6b8cf84439d57cb106f03353.svg) is an orthogonal basis for $V.$" :tutorial/id #uuid "3b833ab7-f6d4-5c93-8709-37ecf29bf023" :tutorial/math-academy-id 3631 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "e23dc2ed-aace-586d-8f71-e7621bc6d386" :step/math-academy-id 20257 :step/next {:db/id 17592186134685}} {:db/id 17592186135054 :tutorial/content "The **Gram-Schmidt process** is an algorithm that we can use to construct an *orthogonal* basis if we are given a non-orthogonal basis to start with.

A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -3 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 5\end{aligned}],\,B={[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]}
$$

Consider the subspace $\text{Col}(A)$ and an orthogonal basis $B$ of $\text{Col}(A),$ where $A$ and $B$ are given above. Given that $B$ is derived from $\text{Col}(A)$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, what is the value of $\frac{b}{a}?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that $\text{Col}(A)$ is the span of the columns of $A.$  

First, let's denote

$\,$ ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2 \\ 5\end{aligned}].$ 

We proceed to find an orthogonal basis using the Gram-Schmidt process, as follows.

**Step 1**: We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

**Step 2**: Next, we find ${v}_{2}$, by using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for ${v}_{2}$ in our case gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{(-3)\cdot (-2)+2\cdot 1+5\cdot 2}{(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 2 \\ 5\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $B={{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}={[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}$ is an orthogonal basis for $\text{Col}(A).$

Finally, $a=1,$ $b=0,$ and

$$

"q-41971" :question/problem "$$
V=\text{Span}{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4 \\ 2\end{aligned}]},\,B={[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{14}}{7} \\ \frac{\sqrt{14}}{14} \\ \frac{3\sqrt{14}}{14}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]}
$$

Consider the subspace $V$ and an **orthonormal** basis $B$ of $V,$ given above. Given that $B$ is derived from $V$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, what is the value of $|a|+|b|+|c|?$" :question/worked-solution "First, let's denote

$\,$ ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ 

We proceed to find an orthogonal basis using the Gram-Schmidt process, as follows.

**Step 1**: We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$

**Step 2**: Next, we find ${v}_{2}$, by using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for ${v}_{2}$ in our case gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{2\cdot 2+4\cdot 1+2\cdot 3}{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4 \\ 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we normalize each vector to get an orthonormal basis.

- ${u}_{1}=\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{14}}{7} \\ \frac{\sqrt{14}}{14} \\ \frac{3\sqrt{14}}{14}\end{aligned}].$

- ${u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{3}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ \frac{3\sqrt{10}}{10} \\ -\frac{\sqrt{10}}{10}\end{aligned}].$

Therefore, $B={{u}_{1},{u}_{2}}={[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{14}}{7} \\ \frac{\sqrt{14}}{14} \\ \frac{3\sqrt{14}}{14}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ \frac{3\sqrt{10}}{10} \\ -\frac{\sqrt{10}}{10}\end{aligned}]}$ is an orthonormal basis for $V.$

Finally, $a=0,$ $b=\frac{3\sqrt{10}}{10},$ $c=-\frac{\sqrt{10}}{10}$ and  

$$
|a|+|b|+|c|=|\,0\,|+|\frac{3\sqrt{10}}{10}|+|-\frac{\sqrt{10}}{10}|=\frac{2\sqrt{10}}{5}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "74c122ae-6f5f-55d9-980e-db9851e51f87" :step/next {:db/id 17592186414754}} {:db/id 17592186414756 :step/content {:db/id 17592186134311 :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "012fe31e-f759-58b8-9e32-2deea745562c" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{2}{3}" :db/id 17592186414720} {:answer/id #uuid "5a5c8c62-d50c-5ae9-8f35-24b24fc3d1ae" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{7}{3}" :db/id 17592186414728} {:answer/id #uuid "632c6ed4-e8c2-5396-8c74-4461b4fdfa46" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{5}{3}" :db/id 17592186414731} {:answer/id #uuid "862d3a52-49ed-5b27-bb35-bc67945b8d32" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{8}{3}" :db/id 17592186414736} {:answer/id #uuid "94c4a1bf-b64c-5ddd-8ca9-6c65c5b9727e" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "\frac{1}{3}" :db/id 17592186414737}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186414731} :answer-field/id #uuid "4a66add1-170c-5173-8823-07f893271a27" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186414746}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045486} :question/id #uuid "1ad7f9ba-9786-5d27-9e6a-080a7315cce4" :question/math-academy-id "q-40740" :question/problem "$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 \\ -2 & 0 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}],\,B={{u}_{1},{u}_{2}}={[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]}
$$

Consider the subspace $\text{Col}(A)$ and an **orthonormal** basis $B$ of $\text{Col}(A),$ where $A$ and $B$ are given above. Given that $B$ is derived from $\text{Col}(A)$ using the Gram-Schmidt process, what is the value of $|a|+|b|+|c|?$" :question/worked-solution "Recall that $\text{Col}(A)$ is the span of the columns of $A.$  

First, let's denote

$\,$ ${a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ -3\end{aligned}].$ 

We proceed to find an orthogonal basis using the Gram-Schmidt process, as follows.

**Step 1**: We set ${v}_{1}={a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

**Step 2**: Next, we find ${v}_{2}$, by using the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{{a}_{2}\cdot {v}_{1}}{{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}}{v}_{1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the formula for ${v}_{2}$ in our case gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2} & ={a}_{2}-\frac{3\cdot (-1)+0\cdot (-2)+(-3)\cdot 2}{{1}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}}{v}_{1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ -3\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we normalize each vector to get an orthonormal basis:

- ${u}_{1}=\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{2}^{2}}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}].$

- ${u}_{2}=\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3} \\ -\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}].$

Therefore, $B={{u}_{1},{u}_{2}}={[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3} \\ \frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3} \\ -\frac{2}{3} \\ -\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}]}$ is an orthonormal basis for $\text{Col}(A).$

Finally, $a=\frac{2}{3},$ $b=-\frac{2}{3},$ $c=-\frac{1}{3}$ and  

$$
|a|+|b|+|c|=|\frac{2}{3}|+|-\frac{2}{3}|+|-\frac{1}{3}|=\frac{5}{3}.
$$"} :step/id #uuid "84989845-fb61-500c-b47d-0a19bc3d185f" :step/next {:db/id 17592186414755}} {:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "012fe31e-f759-58b8-9e32-2deea745562c" :answer/type {:db/id :question.difficulty/easy} :question/problem "$$
[T]_{C}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}],\,{P}_{C\to B}=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $[T]_{C}$ of a linear transformation $T$ with respect to the basis $C$ and the change-of-coordinates matrix ${P}_{C\to B}$ shown above. Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $B.$" :question/worked-solution "The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the bases $B$ and $C$ is given by the following diagram:

![](images/2e/2e82c232614bec8a98f079ea56d7913ee13e7b457e33e418198278d2e369fc5c.png)

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{C}={P}_{C\to B}^{-1}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{C\to B}.
$$

where ${P}_{C\to B}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $C$ to $B.$

Our goal is to compute $[T]_{B}.$ Solving this equation for $[T]_{B},$ we obtain the alternative formulation

$$
[T]_{B}={P}_{C\to B}\cdot [T]_{C}\cdot {P}_{C\to B}^{-1}.
$$

First, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{C\to B}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{C\to B}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-1)\cdot (-5)-3\cdot 2}[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ -3 & -5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{B} & ={P}_{C\to B}\cdot [T]_{C}\cdot {P}_{C\to B}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 3 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 7 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186395236 :question/id #uuid "4f59fe0b-284b-5212-bd9c-6b6ffbb22f39" :question/math-academy-id "q-97116"} {:db/id 17592186419683 :question/id #uuid "426fab7e-1490-581a-8c87-fe143e595ca4" :question/math-academy-id "q-140453" :question/answer-fields [{:answer-field/choices [{:answer/id #uuid "3cd07fe6-6fc8-5bf5-a02a-2d9be90b12af" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}7 & 6 \\ -14 & -10\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186419666} {:answer/id #uuid "5e5ddfaa-301e-59f4-a460-764955ae24fe" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}10 & 6 \\ -14 & -7\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186419668} {:answer/id #uuid "6431b86f-886e-5d1c-a26b-505391b5eaa1" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}10 & -6 \\ 14 & 9\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186419669} {:answer/id #uuid "9029cfa0-da2b-5680-a6e9-bd10f503ed2f" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}6 & 10 \\ -14 & -7\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186419672} {:answer/id #uuid "b7bd80ae-8e71-5474-9567-c47f73ef5af4" :answer/type {:db/id 17592186045498} :answer/value "[\begin{aligned}10 & -7 \\ -14 & 6\end{aligned}]" :db/id 17592186419673}] :answer-field/correct {:db/id 17592186419668} :answer-field/id #uuid "80639a3b-2c96-57ee-bd01-981e0851478b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type {:db/id 17592186045493} :db/id 17592186419682}] :question/difficulty {:db/id 17592186045485} :question/problem "$$

$$

Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C.$" :question/worked-solution "The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the bases $B$ and $C$ is given by the following diagram:

![](images/1b/1b81504d6fdcabee0e1f586fef3dd2af5a57a8411ba4d22429e00e09b171a4d1.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1}\,,
$$

where ${P}_{B\to C}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$

Our goal is to compute $[T]_{C}.$ First, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1\cdot 1-(-2)\cdot (-1)}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can compute the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 4 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -4 \\ 0 & 7\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 & 6 \\ -14 & -7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$"} {:db/id 17592186480634 :question/id #uuid "090d811d-2518-5f77-a8e6-7fb33e3ee0bb" :question/math-academy-id "q-97113"} {:db/id 17592186129131 :knowledge-point/canonical-example {:db/id $$
[T]_{S}={P}_{B\to S}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to S}^{-1},

$$
{P}_{B\to S}=[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}].

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to S}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4\cdot (-1)-(-1)\cdot 5}[\begin{aligned}-1 & -5 \\ 1 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -5 \\ 1 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Find the matrix of $T$ relative to the basis $C.$" :question/worked-solution "The connection between the matrices of our linear transformation $T$ relative to the bases $B$ and $C$ is given by the following diagram:

![](images/1b/1b81504d6fdcabee0e1f586fef3dd2af5a57a8411ba4d22429e00e09b171a4d1.png)

 

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. Algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[T]_{C}={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1},
$$

where ${P}_{B\to C}$ is the change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C.$

First, let's denote the vectors of $B$ and $C$ as ${{b}_{1},{b}_{2}}$ and ${{c}_{1},{c}_{2}}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of vectors from $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ To do this, we consider the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

We reduce $M$ using Gaussian elimination until we get the identity matrix on the left. By doing this, we obtain the required change-of-coordinates matrix on the right.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 11 & 6 \\ -1 & 1 & -5 & -3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 11 & 6 \\ 0 & 3 & 6 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 11 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-2){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 7 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
{P}_{B\to C}=[\begin{aligned}7 & 4 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we compute the inverse of ${P}_{B\to C}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{B\to C}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}7 & 4 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =\frac{1}{1\cdot 7-2\cdot 4}[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ -2 & 7\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 \\ 2 & -7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $B$ to $C$ is a matrix whose columns are the coordinates of vectors from $B$ relative to the basis $C.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of ${b}_{1}$ and ${b}_{2}$ relative to the basis $C.$ To do this, we consider the matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}| & | & | & | \\ {c}_{1} & {c}_{2} & {b}_{1} & {b}_{2} \\ | & | & | & |\end{aligned}].
$$

We reduce $M$ using Gaussian elimination until we get the identity matrix on the left. By doing this, we obtain the required change-of-coordinates matrix on the right.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & -3 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & -2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 4 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

:activity/steps [{:db/id 17592186129967 :step/content {:db/id 17592186130348 :tutorial/content "Recall that the matrices $[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}$ and $[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}$ of a linear transformation $\mathbf{T} : V \to V$ relative to two bases $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ and $\color{red}\mathcal{C}$ of a vector space $V$ are different.

If we are given the matrix $[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}},$ how do we find the matrix $[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}?$
To find $[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{red}\mathcal{C}},$ we use the change-of-coordinates matrix $P_{\small {\color{blue}\mathcal{B}} \to {\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}$ from $\color{blue}\mathcal{B}$ to ${\color{red}\mathcal{C}}.$

The diagram below is a commutative diagram that shows how a change of basis works at each step.

![](images/df/dff02d9f46eb7ded23f418765a50dd1971145cd0e585a82beeef1a45812df8a7.png)

Here, moving along an arrow means pre-multiplying by the corresponding matrix. So algebraically, we can write this as

$$
[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{red}\mathcal{C}} = P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}} \cdot [\mathbf{T}]_{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}} \cdot P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}^{-1}.
$$

For instance, if ![](images/89/89530292f17bb402acb489d90a17e7628a33bab37165b02580479b116e6a2b23.svg) and ![](images/f7/f75100cf6de9ccdb537d685f4e2858278214bbe351c9828e8a94a58628c1151b.svg), we use this formula to obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}[T]_{C} & ={P}_{B\to C}\cdot [T]_{B}\cdot {P}_{B\to C}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 7 \\ -2 & -3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the formula for $[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}},$ we obtain the alternative formulation

$$
[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}} = P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}^{-1} \cdot [\mathbf{T}]_{\color{red}\mathcal{C}} \cdot P_{\small{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}\to{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}}.
$$

**Note:** Alternatively, if we know the change-of-coordinates matrix $P_{\small {\color{red}\mathcal{C}} \to {\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}}$ from $\color{red}\mathcal{C}$ to $\color{blue}\mathcal{B},$ we can construct a similar diagram:

![](images/d6/d6cd195ccd42804ea91debabd23563bb0f6903fdd1b5d708b712c75417fff2a9.png)

From this, we can derive the equation

$$
[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{red}\mathcal{C}} = P_{\small{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}\to{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}}^{-1} \cdot [\mathbf{T}]_{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}} \cdot P_{\small{\color{red}\mathcal{C}}\to{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}}}.
$$

Solving this equation for $[\mathbf{T}]_{\color{blue}\mathcal{B}},$ we obtain the alternative formulation

$$
